description: Atropatene was an ancient Iranian kingdom founded around 323 BC in the rugged highlands of north-western Iran by the former Persian satrap Atropates. The dynasty successfully preserved Zoroastrian religious traditions and Iranian political culture free from direct Hellenistic Macedonian administration, maintaining sovereign statehood for over a century until becoming a subordinate client of the expanding Seleucid Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ganzak; Common languages: Old Persian, Median; Religion: Zoroastrianism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Atropatid; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 323 BC; Disestablished: 223 BC

name: Maurya Empire
description: The Maurya Empire was an expansive Iron Age imperial state founded around 323 BC by Chandragupta Maurya in the historic Gangetic realm of Magadha. Administered from the magnificent fortified metropolis of Pataliputra with the strategic counsel of Chanakya, the empire rapidly expanded across the northern subcontinent, repulsing Seleucid forces and absorbing territory from modern Afghanistan to the Deccan. Reaching its moral and cultural zenith under Emperor Ashoka, who patronised Buddhism and inscribed ethical edicts across his realm, the empire governed as a dominant pan-Indian power until internal fragmentation precipitated its collapse in 180 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Pataliputra; Common languages: Magadhi Prakrit, Sanskrit; Religion: Buddhism, Hinduism, Jainism; Government: Autocratic monarchy; Ruler title: Samrat; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 323 BC; Disestablished: 180 BC

name: Thebai
label: greek poleis
description: Thebai, historically designated as Phthiotic Thebes, was an influential Greek maritime polis situated in the coastal lowlands of Achaia Phthiotis in south-eastern Thessaly. Operating its maritime trade through the adjacent port of Pyrasus on the Pagasetic Gulf, the city flourished as the premier commercial emporium of the region. The city maintained its municipal autonomy and civic magistracies throughout the tumultuous Diadochi conflicts until becoming incorporated into the expanding federal network of the Aetolian League during the third century BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Thebai; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: City-state republic; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 322 BC; Disestablished: 250 BC; Historical region: Thessaly

name: Kingdom of Polyperchon
label: diadochi
description: The Kingdom of Polyperchon was a short-lived Macedonian regency state established in 319 BC following the death of Antipater, who had nominated the veteran general Polyperchon as supreme regent of the Argead Empire. Struggling to protect the royal heirs against the rival ambitions of Cassander, Polyperchon allied with Queen Olympias and promulgated a famous imperial edict restoring democratic liberties across Greek poleis. Operating primarily from his stronghold at Megalopolis in the Peloponnese, his regency authority dissolved in 317 BC after military reverses forced him to surrender control of Macedonia. \n\n Status: Sovereign regency; Administrative seat: Megalopolis; Common languages: Ancient Macedonian, Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Imperial regency; Ruler title: Regent; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 319 BC; Disestablished: 317 BC; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Cassander

name: Kingdom of Cassander
label: diadochi
description: The Kingdom of Cassander was a Hellenistic monarchy founded in 316 BC when Antipater's ruthless son Cassander seized control of Macedonia and southern Greece during the Wars of the Diadochi. Establishing his royal capital at the newly founded maritime city of Thessalonica, Cassander eliminated the surviving Argead royal lineage and proclaimed himself king in 305 BC. The Antipatrid regime concentrated on economic reconstruction, urban foundations and northern border fortification, sustaining royal power across mainland Greece until domestic succession disputes enabled Demetrius Poliorcetes to overthrow the dynasty in 294 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Thessalonica; Common languages: Ancient Macedonian, Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Antipatrid dynasty; Ruler title: Basileus; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 316 BC; Disestablished: 294 BC

name: Kingdom of Lysimachus
label: diadochi
description: The Kingdom of Lysimachus was a major Hellenistic successor state created by Alexander the Great's former bodyguard Lysimachus, initially encompassing Thrace and the Black Sea straits. Establishing a monumental capital at Lysimachia on the Thracian Chersonese, Lysimachus assumed the royal title in 306 BC and dramatically expanded his realm across western Asia Minor following the defeat of Antigonus at Ipsus in 301 BC. Later seizing Macedonia itself, the vast monarchy unravelled through lethal court intrigues, culminating in Lysimachus's defeat and death at the Battle of Corupedium in 281 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Lysimachia; Common languages: Ancient Greek, Thracian; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Basileus; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 316 BC; Disestablished: 282 BC; Preceded by: Macedonian Empire

name: Kingdom of Macedon
label: diadochi
description: The Kingdom of Macedon was the enduring Hellenistic realm governed by the Antigonid dynasty, who rose to prominence under Antigonus I Monophthalmus and his son Demetrius Poliorcetes. Centred on the traditional royal seat of Pella, the monarchy commanded formidable sarissa-wielding phalanxes and exercised broad hegemony over southern Greece through strategic garrisons. The Antigonid kings maintained Macedon as a premier European power and tenaciously contested regional supremacy against rival Diadochi until Roman legions finally extinguished the kingdom at Pydna in 168 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Pella; Common languages: Ancient Macedonian, Koine Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Antigonid dynasty; Ruler title: Basileus; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 316 BC; Disestablished: 169 BC

name: Ptolemaic Kingdom
label: diadochi
description: The Ptolemaic Kingdom was a wealthy Hellenistic empire founded in Egypt by Alexander the Great's Macedonian general Ptolemy I Soter. Governed from the cosmopolitan Mediterranean metropolis of Alexandria, the dynasty harmonised Greek administrative institutions with traditional Egyptian pharaonic kingship, presenting themselves as living gods to their native subjects. Renowned as a pre-eminent centre of scholarship, maritime commerce and naval power through institutions like the Library of Alexandria, the kingdom held sway over Cyprus and the Levant until Cleopatra VII's defeat in 30 BC ushered in Roman rule. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Alexandria; Common languages: Koine Greek, Demotic Egyptian; Religion: Hellenistic religion, Ancient Egyptian religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ptolemaic dynasty; Ruler title: Pharaoh; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 316 BC; Disestablished: 30 BC

name: League of the Islanders
label: antique greek leagues
description: The League of the Islanders was a federal koinon uniting the Aegean city-states of the Cyclades under the direct patronage and suzerainty of the Antigonid kingdom of Macedon. Organised around 314 BC by Antigonus I Monophthalmus to challenge rival Ptolemaic naval ambitions, the league established its administrative and religious headquarters at the pan-Hellenic sanctuary of Delos. Member island poleis sent delegates to a federal synedrion that coordinated collective naval defence, contributed financial subsidies and proclaimed divine honours for their Macedonian royal protectors. \n\n Status: Vassal confederation; Administrative seat: Delos; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Federal league; Legislature: Synedrion; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 314 BC; Disestablished: 287 BC; Historical region: Aegean Islands

name: Seleucid Kingdom
label: diadochi
description: The Seleucid Kingdom was an immense Hellenistic empire established in 312 BC by the Macedonian commander Seleucus I Nicator across the vast Asian territories of Alexander the Great's former realm. Moving its political centre from Mesopotamia to the newly founded capital of Antioch on the Orontes, the dynasty founded dozens of Greek poleis and maintained royal authority over an exceptionally diverse multi-ethnic population. Despite enduring frequent dynastic wars with Ptolemaic Egypt and losing its eastern provinces to the Parthians, the kingdom preserved Hellenistic civilisation in Syria until Roman annexation in 63 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Antioch; Common languages: Koine Greek, Aramaic, Old Persian; Religion: Hellenistic religion, Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Seleucid dynasty; Ruler title: Basileus; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 314 BC; Disestablished: 83 BC

name: Kingdom of the Siraces
description: The Kingdom of the Siraces was a prominent Hellenised Sarmatian tribal monarchy centred in the fertile Kuban River basin north of the Caucasus Mountains. Renowned for their formidable armoured cavalry and prosperous trade networks with Pontic Greek cities, the Siraces grew exceptionally wealthy by facilitating commerce between Central Asia and the Black Sea. Under dynasts like King Aripharnes, the realm actively intervened in the dynastic wars of the neighbouring Bosporan Kingdom, maintaining regional autonomy and nomadic martial traditions until Roman and Alanic pressures dissolved the state. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Krasnodar; Common languages: Sarmatian, Ancient Greek; Religion: Scythian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 310 BC; Disestablished: 194 AD; Historical region: Caucasus

name: League of the Islanders
label: antique greek leagues
description: During this era of Aegean naval supremacy, the League of the Islanders operated as a dependent maritime federation subordinate to the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt. Wrested from Antigonid control around 308 BC by Ptolemy I Soter, the league assembled at the sacred island of Delos, where Ptolemaic nesiarchs oversaw federal deliberations and collected naval contributions. The allied Cycladic islanders instituted elaborate royal cults and athletic festivals in honour of the Ptolemaic monarchs, serving as a vital naval bulwark for Alexandrian power until Egyptian influence waned in the mid-third century BC. \n\n Status: Vassal confederation; Administrative seat: Delos; Common languages: Koine Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Federal league under Ptolemaic nesiarch; Ruler title: Nesiarch; Legislature: Synedrion; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 308 BC; Disestablished: 245 BC

name: Kingdom of Iberia
description: The Kingdom of Iberia was an ancient Georgian monarchy established around 302 BC in the fertile valleys of the Kura River across modern eastern Georgia. Founded by King Pharnavaz I, who unified the disparate Kartvelian tribes and built the fortified royal acropolis of Armazi, the kingdom developed an early administrative network divided into saeristavo provinces. Navigating complex geopolitical rivalries between the Roman Empire and regional Iranian powers, Iberia maintained its sovereign institutions, distinctive script and cultural autonomy as the historic precursor to medieval unified Georgia. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Armazi; Common languages: Old Georgian, Greek, Aramaic; Religion: Georgian paganism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Pharnavazid dynasty; Ruler title: Mepe; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 302 BC; Historical region: Caucasus

name: Kingdom of Demetrius
label: diadochi
description: The Kingdom of Demetrius was a dynamic Hellenistic maritime domain ruled by Demetrius I Poliorcetes between his defeat at the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BC and his accession to the throne of Macedon in 294 BC. Supported by an invincible war fleet and garrisoned island bastions across the Aegean, Demetrius maintained an armed mobile court without a fixed terrestrial capital. The charismatic monarch leveraged his naval supremacy to liberate Athens, wage coastal campaigns against Cassander and preserve the royal Antigonid cause until seizing supreme power in Macedonia. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Administrative seat: Mobile court; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Antigonid dynasty; Ruler title: Basileus; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 302 BC; Disestablished: 294 BC

name: Kingdom of Pleistarchus
label: diadochi
description: The Kingdom of Pleistarchus was an ephemeral Hellenistic principality created in south-western Anatolia following the decisive partition of the Antigonid realm after the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BC. Granted to Pleistarchus, the brother of King Cassander of Macedonia, the small state encompassed strategic coastal districts in Caria and Cilicia, centring its administration at Heraclea by Latmus. The dynast struggled to entrench his authority against aggressive naval incursions launched by Demetrius Poliorcetes, losing his sovereign holdings within a single year as regional powers dismantled the enclave. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Heraclea by Latmus; Common languages: Ancient Greek, Carian; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Antipatrid dynasty; Ruler title: Dynast; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 302 BC; Disestablished: 302 BC

name: Kingdom of Pontus
description: The Kingdom of Pontus was a powerful Hellenistic monarchy established along the southern coast of the Black Sea by Mithridates I Ktistes around 302 BC. Governed by the Persian-descended Mithridatic dynasty from their initial mountain redoubt at Amaseia and later the coastal port of Sinope, the kingdom forged a unique syncretism of Greek civic culture, Anatolian traditions and Iranian royal ritual. Reaching imperial proportions under Mithridates VI Eupator, the kingdom waged three titanic wars against the Roman Republic before its defeat and partition in 63 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Amaseia; Common languages: Koine Greek, Persian, Anatolian languages; Religion: Hellenistic religion, Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Mithridatic dynasty; Ruler title: Basileus; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 302 BC; Disestablished: 63 BC

name: Chaleion
label: greek poleis
description: Chaleion was an ancient Greek coastal polis belonging to the Ozolian Locrians, situated on the northern shore of the Corinthian Gulf near the modern port of Galaxidi. The community maintained an active merchant fleet and engaged in extensive regional diplomacy, notably ratifying an agreement of sympoliteia with the neighbouring city of Tritaea to share reciprocal landholding and residential rights. The polis preserved its municipal self-governance and local magistrates at the close of the fourth century BC before broader federal alliances absorbed the township. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Chaleion; Common languages: Northwest Doric Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: City-state republic; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 301 BC; Disestablished: 300 BC; Historical region: Central Greece

name: Hippana
label: greek poleis
description: Hippana was an ancient fortified Sicilian polis perched atop the commanding heights of Monte dei Cavalli in the interior hills of western Sicily. Controlling the vital overland route between Panormus and Agrigentum, the city boasted an impressive stone theatre constructed in the late fourth century BC and possessed substantial civic ramparts. The polis preserved its municipal independence and defended its agricultural territory until the First Punic War, when Roman legions besieged and destroyed the mountain citadel in 258 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Hippana; Common languages: Ancient Greek, Sicanian; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: City-state republic; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 301 BC; Disestablished: 258 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Republic; Historical region: Magna Graecia

name: Methana
label: greek poleis
description: Methana was an ancient Greek polis situated on the rugged volcanic peninsula of the same name projecting into the Saronic Gulf from the north-eastern coast of the Argolid. Guarding maritime approaches between Aegina, Troezen and Athens, the city developed robust stone fortifications along its volcanic crags and supported an economy based on terraced viticulture and coastal fishing. The settlement functioned as an autonomous city-state at the turn of the third century BC prior to becoming an important naval base for Ptolemaic operations in Greece. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Methana; Common languages: Doric Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: City-state republic; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 301 BC; Disestablished: 300 BC; Historical region: Peloponnese

name: Mytistratos
label: greek poleis
description: Mytistratos was a heavily fortified ancient inland polis situated upon the precipitous summit of Monte Castellazzo near modern Marianopoli in central Sicily. Celebrated by ancient chroniclers as an almost impregnable mountain redoubt, the city held immense strategic importance during the protracted conflicts between Syracuse, Carthage and Rome. The community governed its own municipal affairs until the First Punic War, when Roman legions under consul Aulus Atilius Caiatinus captured the stronghold in 258 BC after an exhaustive siege, expelling and enslaving the surviving populace. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Mytistratos; Common languages: Ancient Greek, Sicanian; Religion: Polytheism; Government: City-state republic; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 301 BC; Disestablished: 258 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Republic; Historical region: Magna Graecia

name: Âu Việt Confederation
description: The Âu Việt Confederation was an indigenous alliance of upland Baiyue tribes inhabiting the rugged mountain valleys of modern northern Vietnam and neighbouring Guangxi. Possessing sophisticated bronze metallurgic techniques and mastery over terraced highland agriculture, the confederacy maintained extensive barter networks and commercial relations with the lowland Lạc Việt of the Red River Delta. Governed by elected tribal chieftains from their principal mountain settlement at modern Cao Bằng, the alliance flourished until chieftain Thục Phán defeated the Hùng kings in 258 BC to establish the unified state of Âu Lạc. \n\n Status: Tribal confederation; Capital: Cao Bằng; Common languages: Kra-Dai languages; Religion: Traditional animism; Government: Tribal chieftaincy; Ruler title: Chieftain; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 300 BC; Disestablished: 258 BC; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Âu Lạc

name: Gangaridai
description: Gangaridai was a formidable ancient monarchy that ruled the lush alluvial expanse of the lower Ganges Delta across modern Bengal and Bangladesh. Renowned throughout Greco-Roman literature for commanding an invincible armada of thousands of armoured war elephants, the kingdom's military repute played a decisive role in deterring the mutinous troops of Alexander the Great from crossing the Hyphasis. Operating from their thriving riverine emporium of Gange, the rulers oversaw international maritime commerce across the Bay of Bengal until imperial Mauryan expansion gradually integrated the delta. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Gange; Common languages: Prakrit, Sanskrit; Religion: Early Hinduism, Animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 300 BC; Disestablished: 280 BC; Succeeded by: Maurya Empire

name: Jin
description: Jin was an ancient Korean confederacy of proto-historic statelets that occupied the southern half of the Korean peninsula south of the Han River. Bordering the Kingdom of Gojoseon to the north, the league developed advanced bronze casting and early iron technology while engaging in maritime barter with coastal communities in western Japan and China. Lacking a centralised royal capital, the constituent tribes governed through local clan elders until growing political decentralisation gave rise to the three successor Samhan confederacies around the first century BC. \n\n Status: Tribal confederation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Proto-Korean, Peninsular Japonic; Religion: Korean shamanism; Government: Tribal confederacy; Historical era: Bronze and Iron Age; Established: 300 BC; Disestablished: 100 BC; Succeeded by: Samhan

name: Kingdom of Mauretania
description: The Kingdom of Mauretania was an independent Berber monarchy established by the indigenous Mauri people across the coastal mountain belts of modern northern Morocco and north-western Algeria. Governed from regional royal seats at Volubilis and Iol, local monarchs like King Baga maintained a powerful pastoral and mercantile state that supplied prized cavalry forces across the western Mediterranean. The kingdom vigorously defended its sovereignty through shifting diplomatic pacts with Carthage, Numidia and Rome until becoming transformed into a Roman client state under King Juba II in 25 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Iol; Common languages: Berber, Punic, Latin; Religion: Traditional Berber religion, Punic polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Agellid; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 300 BC; Disestablished: 25 BC; Historical region: North Africa

name: Thaton Kingdom
label: mon kingdoms
description: The Thaton Kingdom was an influential Mon realm, historically remembered as Suwarnabhumi, centred upon the maritime coastal city of Thaton in Lower Burma. Fostering intensive oceanic trade with ancient Sri Lanka and the Coromandel Coast of India, the kingdom served as the paramount cradle of Theravada Buddhism and Pali scholarship in early mainland South-East Asia. Governed by pious Mon dynasties who patronised magnificent brick pagodas, the coastal monarchy flourished for over a millennium until King Anawrahta of Pagan conquered the city in May 1057. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Thaton; Common languages: Mon; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical antiquity to post-classical era; Established: 300 BC; Disestablished: 17 May 1057; Succeeded by: Pagan Kingdom

name: Tribal Federation of the Masaesyli
description: The Tribal Federation of the Masaesyli was an influential western Numidian Berber confederation situated across the fertile coastal valleys of modern western Algeria. Governing from their primary royal redoubt at Siga near the mouth of the Tafna River, the confederacy maintained an uneasy political relationship resembling a protectorate under the Carthaginian Republic. Carthage utilised skilled diplomatic intervention and subsidies to harness the Masaesylian light cavalry against internal African revolts while balancing tribal loyalties until local kings reasserted complete autonomy during the Second Punic War. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Carthage; Capital: Siga; Common languages: Numidian, Punic; Religion: Traditional Berber religion, Punic polytheism; Government: Confederate monarchy; Ruler title: Agellid; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 300 BC; Disestablished: 237 BC

name: Tribal Federation of the Massylii
description: The Tribal Federation of the Massylii was a prominent eastern Numidian tribal union that occupied the plateau country between western Tunisia and eastern Algeria. Ruled by hereditary kings from their inland cliff capital of Cirta, the confederation maintained close political and economic alignments with neighbouring Carthage, functioning under an informal Carthaginian protectorate. The Punic senate relied upon the celebrated Massylian cavalry as elite mercenary contingents in its overseas wars, maintaining suzerainty through royal marriages and subsidies until the Truceless War disrupted Carthaginian control. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Carthage; Capital: Cirta; Common languages: Numidian, Punic; Religion: Traditional Berber religion, Punic polytheism; Government: Confederate monarchy; Ruler title: Agellid; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 300 BC; Disestablished: 237 BC

name: Tribal State of the Scordisci
description: The Tribal State of the Scordisci was a formidable warrior polity formed around the confluence of the Danube and Sava rivers across modern Serbia and eastern Slavonia. Originating from Gallic warbands that settled in the central Balkans following the Celtic invasion of Greece, the Scordisci absorbed indigenous Thracian and Illyrian populations while fortifying their primary tribal oppidum at Singidunum. The tribal federation dominated regional trade routes and defeated multiple Roman consular armies until sustained Roman campaigns under Augustus finally subjugated the territory. \n\n Status: Tribal state; Capital: Singidunum; Common languages: Celtic, Illyrian, Thracian; Religion: Celtic polytheism; Government: Tribal confederation; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 300 BC; Disestablished: 12 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Empire

name: Yelang
description: Yelang was an ancient indigenous kingdom established across the rugged karstic mountains and river valleys of modern western Guizhou in south-western China. Inhabited by non-Han peoples celebrated for distinctive bronze casting and intricate funerary customs, the state prospered by controlling overland trade routes connecting the Sichuan Basin with the South China Sea. The kingdom preserved sovereign autonomy under native dynasts for over two centuries until military expeditions launched under Emperor Wu of Han annexed the mountainous territory into the Han empire in 111 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Yelang; Common languages: Kra-Dai languages, Tibeto-Burman languages; Religion: Traditional animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 300 BC; Disestablished: 111 BC; Succeeded by: Han dynasty

name: Kingdom of Bithynia
description: The Kingdom of Bithynia was an ancient Hellenistic monarchy situated along the Black Sea and Propontis littoral of north-western Anatolia. Formally established in 297 BC when the local ruler Zipoetes I assumed the royal title of basileus, the kingdom reached remarkable commercial prosperity following the foundation of the magnificent port capital of Nicomedia. Successive dynasts skilfully balanced alliances with neighbouring Galatian chieftains and Hellenistic empires to defend their independence until King Nicomedes IV bequeathed his realm to the Roman Republic in 74 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Nicomedia; Common languages: Koine Greek, Bithynian; Religion: Greek polytheism, Anatolian religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bithynian dynasty; Ruler title: Basileus; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 297 BC; Disestablished: 75 BC

name: Euboean League
label: antique greek leagues
description: The Euboean League was a federal sympoliteia uniting the ancient city-states of the island of Euboea, operating from its principal federal centre at Chalcis. Established to coordinate mutual defence and preserve insular autonomy in the turbulent wake of Demetrius Poliorcetes's rule, the confederation maintained a representative federal council, enacted common laws and minted unified silver coinage inscribed with federal monograms. The league steered an independent course through fluctuating Macedonian and Hellenistic alignments until Roman intervention reshaped political structures across central Greece in 196 BC. \n\n Status: Confederal republic; Administrative seat: Chalcis; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Federal republic; Ruler title: Hegemon; Legislature: Federal council; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 288 BC; Disestablished: 196 BC

name: Kingdom of Pergamon
description: The Kingdom of Pergamon was an autonomous Hellenistic state established in 282 BC around the formidable acropolis of Pergamon in north-western Asia Minor. Founded by Philetaerus, a former lieutenant of Lysimachus who secured the royal treasury, the infant realm maintained nominal allegiance to the Seleucid Empire while exercising practical sovereignty over the Caicus River valley. Philetaerus laid the structural and financial foundations of the illustrious Attalid dynasty, deftly using immense wealth to expand fortifications and secure alliances until his successor Eumenes I formally renounced Seleucid suzerainty in 263 BC. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom; Capital: Pergamon; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Attalid dynasty; Ruler title: Dynast; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 282 BC; Disestablished: 263 BC

name: Kingdom of Ptolemy Ceraunus
label: diadochi
description: The Kingdom of Ptolemy Ceraunus was an ephemeral Hellenistic monarchy encompassing Thrace and Macedonia, established in 281 BC by the disinherited eldest son of Ptolemy I Soter. Following the assassination of Seleucus I Nicator, Ptolemy Ceraunus seized the royal diadem and established his administrative seat at Lysimachia on the Thracian Chersonese, ruthlessly eliminating domestic rivals and wedding his half-sister Arsinoe II. His turbulent seventeen-month reign came to a violent end in early 279 BC when invading Celtic hordes routed his Macedonian army and killed the king in battle. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Lysimachia; Common languages: Ancient Macedonian, Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Basileus; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 282 BC; Disestablished: 279 BC; Preceded by: Kingdom of Lysimachus

name: Allies of Epirus
description: The Allies of Epirus formed a wartime confederation of Italiote Greek city-states and indigenous Italic peoples who united under King Pyrrhus of Epirus during the Pyrrhic War. Centred around the wealthy Spartan colony of Tarentum and incorporating Samnite, Lucanian and Bruttian contingents, the coalition mobilised substantial citizen levies and cavalry to halt expanding Roman encroachment in southern Italy. Lacking a centralised administrative seat, the alliance coordinated regional military operations with Epirote phalanxes until Roman battlefield resilience and Pyrrhus's eventual withdrawal dissolved the anti-Roman confederacy. \n\n Status: Military alliance; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Ancient Greek, Oscan; Religion: Polytheism; Government: Military confederation; Ruler title: Hegemon; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 281 BC; Disestablished: 276 BC

name: Dian Kingdom
description: The Dian Kingdom was an ancient non-Han civilisation that flourished around the shores of Lake Dian on the high plateau of central Yunnan. Celebrated for extraordinary lost-wax bronze metallurgy, the kingdom produced intricate bronze drums and cowrie containers that depicted vibrant scenes of cavalry warfare, weaving and sacred animal sacrifices. Guided by hereditary monarchs whose burials featured lavish gold seals and iron weaponry, the state maintained political sovereignty until Emperor Wu of Han annexed the realm in 109 BC, transforming it into the Yizhou commandery. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Jinning; Common languages: Tibeto-Burman languages; Religion: Dian animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 279 BC; Disestablished: 109 BC; Succeeded by: Han dynasty

name: Macedonian Kingdom of the Gauls
label: celtic polities
description: The Macedonian Kingdom of the Gauls was a brief Celtic warrior regime established across Macedonia and the northern Aegean littoral following the devastating Gallic invasion of 279 BC. After defeating and killing King Ptolemy Ceraunus in open battle, Gallic warbands led by chieftains such as Bolgios raided throughout the Balkan countryside and garrisoned strategic centres, including the former royal stronghold of Lysimachia. The predatory barbarian dominion collapsed after two years of widespread devastation when Antigonus II Gonatas shattered the Celtic host at the Battle of Lysimachia in 277 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal kingdom; Capital: Lysimachia; Common languages: Gaulish, Ancient Macedonian; Religion: Celtic polytheism; Government: Tribal military chieftaincy; Ruler title: Chieftain; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 279 BC; Disestablished: 277 BC; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Macedon

name: Kingdom of Tylis
label: celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Tylis was a Celtic monarchy established in inland Thrace by Gallic warriors who turned northward following their defeat at the Battle of Lysimachia in 277 BC. Establishing their fortified capital at Tylis in modern central Bulgaria, kings such as Comontorius and Cavarus exercised martial dominion over native Thracian tribes and exacted substantial annual monetary tributes from the wealthy Greek city of Byzantium. The kingdom minted fine Hellenistic-style silver coinage and endured for over six decades until an indigenous Thracian uprising overthrew and destroyed the realm in 212 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Tylis; Common languages: Gaulish, Thracian, Ancient Greek; Religion: Celtic polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 277 BC; Disestablished: 212 BC; Historical region: Thrace

name: Kingdom of Cyrenaica
label: diadochi
description: The Kingdom of Cyrenaica was an independent Hellenistic monarchy established along the Mediterranean coastline of north-eastern Libya around 271 BC. Originally administered as a Ptolemaic dependency, the province asserted complete sovereignty when its ambitious governor Magas declared himself king and challenged Alexandrian naval dominance across the eastern Mediterranean. The flourishing kingdom fostered elite Greek arts, extensive agricultural trade in valuable silphium and civic patronage in the ancient Dorian city of Cyrene before being peacefully reabsorbed into the Ptolemaic realm upon Magas's death in 250 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Cyrene; Common languages: Doric Greek, Koine Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ptolemaic dynasty; Ruler title: Basileus; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 271 BC; Disestablished: 250 BC

name: Kingdom of Galatia
label: celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Galatia was a prominent Celtic state established across the central Anatolian highlands around modern Ankara by Gallic tribes who crossed the Hellespont in the 270s BC. Divided into three principal tribes, namely the Tolistobogii, Trocmi and Tectosages, the Galatians established fortified hill settlements, instituted a joint council at the sacred oak grove of Drynemeton and frequently served as elite mercenaries for Hellenistic monarchs. Transitioning from a collegiate tribal tetrarchy to a centralised monarchy, the kingdom fiercely preserved its Celtic speech and customs until becoming a Roman client realm in 40 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ancyra; Common languages: Galatian, Koine Greek; Religion: Celtic polytheism; Government: Tribal confederation and monarchy; Ruler title: Tetrarch; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 269 BC; Disestablished: 40 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Kingdom of the Maldives
description: The Kingdom of the Maldives, known in early regional traditions as Dheeva Maari, governed the coral atolls across the central Indian Ocean from antiquity into the high medieval era. Rooted in Theravada Buddhist culture alongside earlier maritime animist beliefs, the island kingdom maintained vital trade links with South India and Ceylon, exporting cowrie shells and dried fish across regional sea lanes. The monarchy endured until the mid-twelfth century, when the royal court embraced Islam under King Dhovemi, transforming the archipelago into a sultanate. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Malé; Common languages: Dhivehi; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Historical era: Antiquity to Early Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1154; Succeeded by: Sultanate of the Maldives

name: Kingdom of Pergamon
description: The Kingdom of Pergamon emerged as a major Hellenistic power in western Anatolia after breaking away from Seleucid overlordship following the Battle of Sardis in 263 BC. Ruled by the Attalid dynasty from their heavily fortified acropolis, the monarchs transformed their capital into a celebrated centre of art, scholarship and monumental architecture that rivalled Alexandria. Maintaining close diplomatic and military ties with the Roman Republic to counter rival Macedonian and Syrian influence, the state lasted until its final ruler bequeathed the realm to Rome, leading to provincial reorganisation in 129 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Pergamon; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Attalid dynasty; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 263 BC; Disestablished: 129 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Syrakousai
label: greek poleis
description: Syrakousai functioned as an autonomous Greek city-state and vital ally of the Roman Republic throughout the middle decades of the third century BC. Guided by the cautious diplomacy of King Hiero II, the wealthy Sicilian metropolis supplied grain and naval support to Roman forces during the First Punic War, securing extensive territorial autonomy across south-eastern Sicily. Following Hiero's death, factional shifts led the polis into an ill-fated alliance with Carthage, culminating in a protracted Roman siege and the violent sack of the city in 212 BC. \n\n Status: Roman ally; Capital: Syracuse; Common languages: Doric Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Disestablished: 213 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Âu Lạc
description: Âu Lạc was an ancient proto-Vietnamese kingdom established in the Red River Delta following the unification of the Âu Việt and Lạc Việt peoples by Thục Phán, who assumed the royal title An Dương Vương. Governed from the massive spiral fortress of Cổ Loa, the kingdom possessed an advanced bronze-working culture characterised by specialised crossbow technology and sophisticated water-control works. Its autonomy came to an abrupt end around 180 BC when the southern Chinese warlord state of Nanyue overwhelmed its defences and annexed the realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Cổ Loa; Common languages: Proto-Vietic; Religion: Animism and ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 258 BC; Disestablished: 180 BC; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nanyue

name: Ardiaean Kingdom
description: The Ardiaean Kingdom was an influential Illyrian realm that flourished along the eastern Adriatic seaboard, dominating coastal trade and maritime routes between the Neretva River and Lake Shkodra. Under dynamic leaders such as King Agron and Queen Teuta, the state developed a formidable naval fleet composed of swift lembi, launching aggressive privateering raids that challenged Greek coastal colonies and Italian commerce. This maritime expansion provoked direct military intervention from the Roman Republic, initiating the Illyrian Wars that ultimately dismantled the kingdom in 168 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Risan; Common languages: Illyrian; Religion: Illyrian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 250 BC; Disestablished: 168 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Dzibilchaltún
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Dzibilchaltún flourished as an enduring Maya urban polity on the northern coastal plain of the Yucatán Peninsula from the Late Preclassic period until the early fourteenth century. Benefiting from coastal salt harvesting and extensive trade routes linking inland settlements to maritime networks, the city developed distinctive monumental architecture, including the famous Temple of the Seven Dolls and extensive sacbeob causeways. The settlement survived regional political collapses that felled southern centres, maintaining civic and ceremonial activity well into the Postclassic era. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Dzibilchaltun; Common languages: Yucatec Maya; Religion: Maya religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Preclassic to Postclassic Mesoamerica; Established: 250 BC; Disestablished: 1301

name: Greco-Bactrian Kingdom
label: seleucid secessionist states;greco-bactrian polities
description: The Greco-Bactrian Kingdom was a prosperous Hellenistic state founded around 250 BC when the Seleucid satrap Diodotus declared independence across Central Asian territories centred in ancient Bactria and Sogdiana. Renowned for its fortified urban centres, rich agricultural plains and prolific Hellenistic coinage, the kingdom blended Greek artistic, administrative and military traditions with Iranian and nomadic cultural elements. Internal dynastic strife and outward expansion into northern India weakened the realm, leaving it vulnerable to successive waves of nomadic invaders who overran its core cities around 120 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bactra; Common languages: Ancient Greek and Bactrian; Religion: Greek polytheism, Buddhism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 250 BC; Disestablished: 120 BC; Succeeded by: Indo-Greek Kingdom and Yuezhi

name: Kuninda Kingdom
description: The Kuninda Kingdom was an ancient Himalayan polity located across the mountainous river valleys of the Yamuna and Sutlej in present-day Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. Functioning as a tribal monarchy or aristocratic confederacy, the Kunindas prospered through the control of lucrative trans-Himalayan trade routes carrying timber, minerals and medicinal herbs to the northern Gangetic plains. The realm minted distinctive silver and copper coinage featuring Buddhist and Shaivite iconography under rulers such as Amoghabhuti, maintaining local autonomy until its eventual integration into the Gupta sphere. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Prakrit and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 250 BC; Disestablished: 251; Succeeded by: Gupta Empire

name: Pandya Kingdom
description: The Pandya Kingdom was one of the legendary three crowned realms of ancient Tamilakam, governing the southernmost regions of the Indian peninsula from its historic capital at Madurai. Renowned for its pearl fisheries in the Gulf of Mannar and bustling maritime commerce with the Hellenistic and Roman worlds, the kingdom fostered early Tamil Sangam literature and civic institutions. Though eclipsed for several centuries during the Kalabhra interregnum, the dynastic lineage successfully revived its authority in the sixth century and maintained a dominant presence across southern India until the fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Madurai; Common languages: Old Tamil; Religion: Hinduism, Jainism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical to Medieval India; Established: 250 BC; Disestablished: 1331; Succeeded by: Madurai Sultanate and Vijayanagara Empire

name: Parthian Empire
description: The Parthian Empire, also known as the Arsacid Empire, was a major Iranian imperial power established in 247 BC when Arsaces I led the nomadic Parni tribe in seizing the north-eastern satrapy of Parthia. Over subsequent decades, the Arsacids expanded across the Iranian plateau and conquered Mesopotamia from the declining Seleucids, establishing Ctesiphon as their winter capital and dominating Silk Road commerce. Balancing Hellenistic administrative heritage with Iranian dynastic traditions and aristocratic feudal assemblies, the empire withstood numerous Roman invasions before falling to the rising Sasanians in 224. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Ctesiphon; Official languages: Parthian; Common languages: Parthian, Koine Greek and Aramaic; Religion: Zoroastrianism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Arsacid dynasty; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 247 BC; Disestablished: 28 April 224; Succeeded by: Sasanian Empire

name: Xiongnu Confederation
description: The Xiongnu Confederation was a powerful nomadic tribal union that dominated the eastern Eurasian steppe and the Mongolian Plateau from the third century BC. Unified into an expansive nomadic empire under supreme leaders such as Modu Chanyu, the confederation fielded formidable horse archers that repeatedly raided the northern frontiers of the Chinese Qin and Han dynasties. Han emperors initially managed the threat through appeasement and tribute treaties known as heqin, but extended military campaigns under Emperor Wu eventually fractured the confederation into rival factions, leading to its gradual dissolution. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal confederation; Capital: Longcheng; Common languages: Yeniseian or Turkic dialects; Religion: Tengrism and Shamanism; Government: Nomadic confederation; Ruler title: Chanyu; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 245 BC; Disestablished: 49; Succeeded by: Han dynasty and Xianbei

name: Kingdom of Antiochus Hierax
label: seleucid secessionist states
description: The Kingdom of Antiochus Hierax was a separatist Hellenistic realm established in western Anatolia during the War of the Brothers, a bitter Seleucid dynastic conflict. Antiochus, nicknamed Hierax for his aggressive ambition, rebelled against his elder brother King Seleucus II Callinicus and asserted sovereign control over territories west of the Taurus Mountains with help from Galatian mercenaries. Ruling from the ancient seat of Sardis, his splinter kingdom disrupted central Seleucid authority for over a decade until combined assaults from Attalus I of Pergamon drove him into exile and brought about his downfall. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Sardis; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Seleucid; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 239 BC; Disestablished: 228 BC; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Pergamon and Seleucid Empire

name: Kingdom of Numidia
description: The Kingdom of Numidia in this initial phase encompassed the tribal Berber territories of north-western Africa operating under the hegemony of ancient Carthage. Divided primarily between the eastern Massylii and western Masaesyli tribal federations, local chieftains supplied Carthage with legendary light cavalry units that played decisive roles in Mediterranean warfare. As the Second Punic War intensified, shifting rivalries between King Syphax and the young Massylian prince Masinissa led the latter to ally with the Roman Republic, setting the stage for Numidian unification and formal independence from Carthaginian control in 202 BC. \n\n Status: Carthaginian vassal kingdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Numidian and Punic; Religion: Traditional Berber religion and Punic polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 237 BC; Disestablished: 202 BC; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Numidia

name: Sena and Guththika
description: Sena and Guththika established a notable joint rule over the Anuradhapura Kingdom in Sri Lanka during the late third century BC after overthrowing the Sinhalese monarch Suratissa. Originally Tamil seafaring merchants and horse traders hailing from southern India, the pair seized the royal citadel and governed the island for over two decades. Traditional chronicles such as the Mahavamsa note that their administration maintained civil order and respected Buddhist institutions despite their foreign origin, until Suratissa's nephew Asela mounted a successful counter-offensive and reclaimed the Sinhalese throne in 215 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign joint monarchy; Capital: Anuradhapura; Common languages: Early Old Tamil and Early Sinhala; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Diarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 237 BC; Disestablished: 215 BC; Succeeded by: Anuradhapura Kingdom

name: Melaina Korkyra
label: greek poleis
description: Melaina Korkyra was a Greek island polis established on the Adriatic island of modern Korčula off the Dalmatian coast, originally colonised by settlers from the Ionian island of Corcyra and later Knidos. Renowned for its dense pine forests and sheltered natural anchorages, the settlement functioned as an autonomous maritime city-state that oversaw vital commercial navigation along the Illyrian coast. Its brief period of complete municipal sovereignty in the late third century BC ended abruptly when expanding Ardiaean Illyrian forces and subsequent Roman naval expeditions intervened across the region in 229 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Melaina Korkyra; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Aristocratic republic; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 231 BC; Disestablished: 229 BC; Succeeded by: Ardiaean Kingdom and Roman Republic

name: State of Dai
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Dai was a northern Chinese rump principality established in 228 BC by Prince Jia of Zhao following the catastrophic fall of the Zhao capital Handan to the invading Qin armies. Escaping to the remote northern frontier commandery around modern Hebei and Shanxi, Jia proclaimed himself King of Dai and maintained resistance alongside local marcher forces and allied state remnants. Dai coordinated with the neighbouring state of Yan in an unsuccessful effort to halt Qin expansion, ultimately collapsing when Qin general Wang Ben marched northward and captured Jia in 222 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign rump kingdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Warring States period; Established: 229 BC; Disestablished: 222 BC; Preceded by: State of Zhao; Succeeded by: Qin dynasty

name: Palenque
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Palenque, known in classic Maya inscriptions as Lakamha, was an influential city-state in southern Mexico positioned along the foothills overlooking the coastal plains of Chiapas. Developing from an agrarian Preclassic village into a sophisticated Classic centre, the city achieved renown for its refined palace architecture, vaulted temples and intricate hieroglyphic records. Under prominent rulers such as K'inich Janaab' Pakal and his descendants, Palenque waged protracted conflicts against rival centres including Calakmul and Toniná, before environmental stress and internal instability triggered its abandonment in the early ninth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Palenque; Common languages: Ch'olan Maya; Religion: Maya religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classic Maya period; Established: 226 BC; Disestablished: 800

name: Kingdom of Molon
label: seleucid secessionist states
description: The Kingdom of Molon was an ephemeral separatist state established in 222 BC when Molon, the Seleucid satrap of Media, led a widespread insurrection across the eastern provinces of the empire. Exploiting deep resentment against the chief minister Hermeias, Molon defeated royal armies sent against him, crossed the Tigris and seized control of Babylonia and the wealthy metropolis of Seleucia on the Tigris. His short-lived sovereignty over Mesopotamia collapsed when the young monarch Antiochus III marched east in person, crushing the rebel forces in pitched battle in 220 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign rebel kingdom; Capital: Seleucia on the Tigris; Common languages: Ancient Greek, Aramaic and Median; Religion: Greek polytheism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 222 BC; Disestablished: 221 BC; Succeeded by: Seleucid Empire

name: Kingdom of Achaeus
label: seleucid secessionist states
description: The Kingdom of Achaeus was a breakaway Hellenistic realm founded in western Asia Minor by the Seleucid general and royal relative Achaeus in 220 BC. Having successfully recovered lost Anatolian territories from King Attalus I of Pergamon on behalf of Antiochus III, Achaeus leveraged his military popularity to assume the royal diadem and rule autonomously from Sardis. His independent domain challenged central Seleucid authority until Antiochus launched a major punitive campaign across the Taurus Mountains, laying siege to Sardis and capturing and executing Achaeus in 213 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign breakaway kingdom; Capital: Sardis; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Seleucid; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 221 BC; Disestablished: 213 BC; Succeeded by: Seleucid Empire

name: Di
description: The Kingdom of Di was one of the short-lived Eighteen Kingdoms established across northern China in 206 BC following the collapse of the Qin dynasty. Created during the post-Qin territorial partition orchestrated by the warlord Xiang Yu, the fief was granted to the former Qin general Dong Yi, who governed northern Shaanxi to guard against potential western incursions. The principality had little time to consolidate its administration, as Liu Bang launched his blitz eastward from the Hanzhong basin in 205 BC, compelling Dong Yi's surrender and annexing the territory into the emerging Han realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign regional kingdom; Capital: Di; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Chu-Han Contention; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 205 BC; Preceded by: Qin dynasty; Succeeded by: Han dynasty

name: Han
label: eighteen kingdoms
description: The Han dynasty was a defining imperial state in Chinese history established by Liu Bang following the collapse of the Qin dynasty and his triumph in the Chu-Han Contention. Governed first from Chang'an during the Western Han and later from Luoyang during the Eastern Han after Wang Mang's brief Xin interregnum, the empire consolidated bureaucratic rule, institutionalised Confucian governance and expanded military frontiers into Central Asia, Korea and northern Vietnam. Its four centuries of commercial prosperity and administrative cohesion established an enduring cultural identity across China before fracturing into the Three Kingdoms in 220. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Chang'an and Luoyang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, Confucianism, Taoism and Buddhism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Liu clan; Historical era: Imperial China; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 11 December 220; Succeeded by: Cao Wei, Shu Han and Eastern Wu

name: Kingdom of Changshan
label: eighteen kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Changshan was a regional realm created in northern China in 206 BC during the territorial partition engineered by Xiang Yu following the Qin dynasty's fall. Bestowed upon the rebel leader Zhang Er with its seat in southern Hebei, the principality encompassed significant portions of the former state of Zhao. The kingdom quickly succumbed to civil conflict when Zhang Er's rival Chen Yu invaded with support from Qi, forcing Zhang Er to seek refuge with Liu Bang, who subsequently absorbed the territory into the Han administrative structure. \n\n Status: Sovereign regional kingdom; Capital: Changshan; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Chu-Han Contention; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 202 BC; Preceded by: Qin dynasty; Succeeded by: Han dynasty

name: Kingdom of Dai
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: The Kingdom of Dai existed briefly in 206 BC as a northern marcher realm during the post-Qin division of China orchestrated by the warlord Xiang Yu. Displacing Zhao Xie from his ancestral Zhao throne, Xiang Yu relegated him to the marginal northern border territory of Dai to neutralise his political influence. Lacking a permanent urban capital, the transient principality dissolved within months when local general Chen Yu drove out Xiang Yu's appointed loyalists, reinstating Zhao Xie over the broader Zhao territories and terminating Dai's separate existence. \n\n Status: Sovereign regional kingdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Chu-Han Contention; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 206 BC; Preceded by: Qin dynasty; Succeeded by: State of Zhao

name: Kingdom of Han
label: eighteen kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Han was an ephemeral principality established in Central China in 206 BC amidst the partition of the fallen Qin Empire into the Eighteen Kingdoms. Xiang Yu initially confirmed the royal descendant Han Cheng over his ancestral lands, but soon deposed and executed him, placing his loyalist general Zheng Chang on the throne. Zheng Chang's rule proved exceedingly brief, as Liu Bang dispatched his general Han Xin into the Yingchuan region later that year, swiftly overcoming local resistance and integrating the territory into the emerging Han domain. \n\n Status: Sovereign regional kingdom; Capital: Hann; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Chu-Han Contention; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 206 BC; Preceded by: Qin dynasty; Succeeded by: Han dynasty

name: Kingdom of Henan
label: eighteen kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Henan was a short-lived regional realm created in 206 BC during the territorial distribution of China overseen by Xiang Yu following the Qin collapse. Centred on the historic Central Plains metropolis of Luoyang, the kingdom was awarded to the insurgent officer Shen Yang for his pivotal role in subduing northern commanderies. Henan held strategic importance along key logistical routes connecting western China to the eastern seaboard, but its independence ended within months when Liu Bang's advancing forces captured Luoyang and secured Shen Yang's capitulation. \n\n Status: Sovereign regional kingdom; Capital: Luoyang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Chu-Han Contention; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 206 BC; Preceded by: Qin dynasty; Succeeded by: Han dynasty

name: Kingdom of Hengshan
label: eighteen kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Hengshan was a regional realm established in the middle Yangtze River basin in 206 BC during Xiang Yu's division of the fallen Qin Empire. The fief was bestowed upon Wu Rui, a widely respected southern magistrate and rebel commander who had assisted in the overthrow of Qin rule, with his seat at modern Huanggang. Maintaining a cautious neutrality before aligning with Liu Bang during the Chu-Han Contention, Wu Rui secured royal favour and was subsequently confirmed as King of Changsha upon the final consolidation of the Han dynasty in 202 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign regional kingdom; Capital: Huanggang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Chu-Han Contention; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 202 BC; Preceded by: Qin dynasty; Succeeded by: Han dynasty

name: Kingdom of Jiaodong
label: eighteen kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Jiaodong was an ephemeral eastern state created in 206 BC on the Shandong Peninsula during Xiang Yu's post-Qin territorial partition. Formed by cleaving the historic lands of Qi into three subordinate entities, the kingdom was assigned to the nominal Qi ruler Tian Shi to weaken regional cohesion. The political arrangement quickly collapsed when the influential general Tian Rong rejected the division, killed Tian Shi for obeying Xiang Yu, and reunited the peninsula under his own command before the year ended. \n\n Status: Sovereign regional kingdom; Capital: Jiaodong; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Chu-Han Contention; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 206 BC; Preceded by: Qin dynasty; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Qi

name: Kingdom of Jibei
label: eighteen kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Jibei was a brief regional polity created across northern Shandong in 206 BC during the fragmentation of the Qin Empire into the Eighteen Kingdoms. Xiang Yu awarded the crown to Tian An, an allied insurgent commander who had captured several cities along the Yellow River, aiming to partition the powerful Qi state into weaker rival principalities. Jibei's separate autonomy proved short-lived, as the disaffected Qi leader Tian Rong attacked within months, killing Tian An and reincorporating Jibei into a unified Qi realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign regional kingdom; Capital: Jibei; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Chu-Han Contention; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 206 BC; Preceded by: Qin dynasty; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Qi

name: Kingdom of Jiujiang
label: eighteen kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Jiujiang was a prominent regional realm in the Huai River valley established in 206 BC following the demise of the Qin dynasty. The kingdom was conferred upon Ying Bu, one of Xiang Yu's most formidable vanguard generals, who set up his capital at the strategic fortress city of Shouchun. Strained relations with Xiang Yu soon drove Ying Bu to switch allegiances, prompting a devastating Chu punitive expedition in 205 BC that compelled him to abandon his domain and join forces with Liu Bang. \n\n Status: Sovereign regional kingdom; Capital: Shouchun; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Chu-Han Contention; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 205 BC; Preceded by: Qin dynasty; Succeeded by: Han dynasty

name: Kingdom of Liaodong
label: eighteen kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Liaodong was an ephemeral northern principality established in 206 BC beyond the Shanhaiguan pass during Xiang Yu's post-Qin reorganisation of China. Xiang Yu relegated the former King of Yan, Han Guang, to this remote north-eastern frontier with his administrative seat at Liaoyang, while rewarding the subordinate general Zang Tu with the wealthier Yan heartland. Han Guang refused to surrender his western territories, prompting Zang Tu to invade Liaodong later that year, killing Han Guang and unifying both realms under his rule. \n\n Status: Sovereign regional kingdom; Capital: Liaoyang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Chu-Han Contention; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 206 BC; Preceded by: Qin dynasty; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Yan

name: Kingdom of Linjiang
label: eighteen kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Linjiang was a regional realm established in southern China along the middle reaches of the Yangtze in 206 BC amidst the dissolution of the Qin Empire. Xiang Yu granted the fief to Gong Ao, an insurgent general from Chu who had led successful military operations in Nan Commandery. Following Gong Ao's death, his son Gong Wei maintained allegiance to Chu during the Chu-Han Contention, staunchly resisting Han advances until royal forces finally captured him in 202 BC, absorbing Linjiang into the Han realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign regional kingdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Chu-Han Contention; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 202 BC; Preceded by: Qin dynasty; Succeeded by: Han dynasty

name: Kingdom of Sai
label: eighteen kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Sai was a short-lived regional state in north-western China established in 206 BC as one of the Three Qins following the fall of the Qin dynasty. Xiang Yu installed Sima Xin, a former senior Qin commander who had surrendered alongside Zhang Han, as king to control the central Guanzhong plain and block the eastern ambitions of Liu Bang. The strategic buffer proved ineffective when Liu Bang broke out of Hanzhong in late 206 BC, compelling Sima Xin's capitulation and dissolving the kingdom into Han commanderies. \n\n Status: Sovereign regional kingdom; Capital: Fenyang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Chu-Han Contention; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 205 BC; Preceded by: Qin dynasty; Succeeded by: Han dynasty

name: Kingdom of Western Chu
label: eighteen kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Western Chu was the hegemonic centre of the post-Qin political order, established in 206 BC by the paramount warlord Xiang Yu after he orchestrated the overthrow of the Qin dynasty. Ruling from the fortified capital of Pengcheng across nine rich eastern commanderies, Xiang Yu styled himself Hegemon-King of Western Chu and oversaw the initial partition of China into the Eighteen Kingdoms. Despite displaying extraordinary battlefield prowess against Han forces, Xiang Yu's diplomatic isolation and logistical disadvantages culminated in his encirclement at Gaixia and suicide in 202 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign hegemonic kingdom; Capital: Pengcheng; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Hegemon-King; Historical era: Chu-Han Contention; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 202 BC; Preceded by: Qin dynasty; Succeeded by: Han dynasty

name: Kingdom of Yin
label: eighteen kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Yin was a regional realm established across northern Henan and southern Hebei in 206 BC during the territorial partition executed by Xiang Yu. Conferred upon Sima Ang, an insurgent Zhao general who had pacified Henei Commandery, the kingdom took its name from the ancient Shang dynasty capital encompassed by the domain. Sima Ang struggled to preserve his independence against neighbouring warlords before being overwhelmed by Liu Bang's vanguard armies in 205 BC, leading to the kingdom's formal absorption into the nascent Han state. \n\n Status: Sovereign regional kingdom; Capital: Anyang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Chu-Han Contention; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 202 BC; Preceded by: Qin dynasty; Succeeded by: Han dynasty

name: Wei
label: northern and southern dynasties (chinese history)
description: Wei designates both the transient regional kingdom ruled by Wei Bao during the Chu-Han Contention and the later Western Wei dynasty that dominated north-western China between 535 and 557. In its sixth-century imperial incarnation, the state emerged from the violent fracture of the Northern Wei, ruling from Chang'an under the nominal authority of Emperor Wen while real political and military power resided with the paramount general Yuwen Tai. The regime instituted the pioneering fubing militia system and reformed northern administrative codes before being formally replaced by the Northern Zhou dynasty. \n\n Status: Sovereign imperial dynasty; Capital: Chang'an; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Xianbei; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Historical era: Northern and Southern dynasties; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 558; Succeeded by: Northern Zhou

name: Kingdom of Qi
description: The Kingdom of Qi was briefly reunified in 206 BC when the insurgent chancellor Tian Rong revolted against Xiang Yu's tripartite division of the Shandong Peninsula. Resentful of being denied a royal title despite his major contributions to the anti-Qin rebellion, Tian Rong mobilised an army, drove out the puppet monarchs of Jiaodong, Jibei and Linzi, and proclaimed himself King of Qi. His defiance precipitated a massive punitive invasion by Xiang Yu, resulting in Tian Rong's defeat and violent retribution across the coastal region. \n\n Status: Sovereign regional kingdom; Capital: Linzi; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Chu-Han Contention; Established: 206 BC; Disestablished: 206 BC; Preceded by: Eighteen Kingdoms; Succeeded by: Han dynasty and Western Chu

name: Kingdom of Nanyue
description: The Kingdom of Nanyue was an expansive southern realm established in 204 BC by the former Qin military commander Zhao Tuo amidst the collapse of the imperial dynasty. Centred at Panyu, in modern Guangzhou, the kingdom encompassed southern China and northern Vietnam, integrating Han Chinese administrative techniques with indigenous Baiyue customs. While maintaining nominal tributary relations with the Han court, Nanyue's rulers frequently asserted imperial autonomy until Emperor Wu launched an overwhelming sea-and-land invasion that conquered the realm and incorporated its territories into Han commanderies in 111 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Panyu; Common languages: Old Chinese and Baiyue languages; Religion: Chinese folk religion and animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Triệu dynasty; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 204 BC; Disestablished: 111 BC; Succeeded by: Han dynasty

name: Kingdom of Numidia
description: The Kingdom of Numidia in this sovereign phase emerged as a unified Berber state in North Africa following Masinissa's decisive alliance with Scipio Africanus during the Second Punic War. Governed from the inland mountain stronghold of Cirta, Masinissa consolidated the Massylian and Masaesylian territories, encouraged sedentary agriculture and urban development, and established a powerful regional realm bordering Carthage. The kingdom flourished through subsequent decades under King Micipsa, maintaining close commercial and diplomatic ties with Rome before dynastic succession disputes triggered the Jugurthine War in the late second century BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Cirta; Common languages: Numidian, Punic and Latin; Religion: Traditional Berber religion and Punic polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Massylian dynasty; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 202 BC; Disestablished: 106 BC; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Numidia (Roman client)

name: Aguateca
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Aguateca was a fortified classic Maya city situated atop a towering ninety-metre limestone cliff overlooking Lake Petexbatún in northern Guatemala. Occupied from the Late Preclassic era, the site served as a vital dual capital alongside Dos Pilas during the Late Classic period, housing elite royal residences, stone monuments and skilled artisans within a dense urban perimeter. Defended by an intricate network of masonry walls and natural chasms, the settlement was nevertheless overrun and sacked around 800 AD, leaving rapid-abandonment archaeological deposits that offer rich insights into daily Maya court life. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Aguateca; Common languages: Classic Maya; Religion: Maya religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Preclassic to Classic Mesoamerica; Established: 200 BC; Disestablished: 801

name: Caucasian Albania
description: Caucasian Albania was an ancient tribal monarchy established across the fertile lowlands and forested valleys of the south-eastern Caucasus, primarily within present-day Azerbaijan. Composed of a confederation of more than two dozen indigenous Caucasian tribes unified under a single monarch, the realm was governed from its fortified capital at Kabalak. The kingdom maintained extensive agricultural production, skilled metallurgy and regional commerce, coexisting alongside neighbouring Caucasian Iberia and Armenia until Roman legions under Pompey intervened in the region in 65 BC, drawing the state into Rome's orbit. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kabalak; Common languages: Caucasian Albanian; Religion: Caucasian Albanian polytheism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 200 BC; Disestablished: 65 BC; Succeeded by: Caucasian Albania (Roman client)

name: Deva Dynasty of Saketa
description: The Deva Dynasty of Saketa was an ancient Indian ruling house that established control over the historic Kosala region from its royal seat at Ayodhya following the decline of the Maurya Empire. Known principally through numismatic discoveries bearing names ending in the honorific suffix deva, these monarchs asserted local sovereignty across the middle Gangetic plains during the second century BC. Their rule preserved regional commerce and religious traditions in Ayodhya until being supplanted by the subsequent Datta dynasty around the turn of the first century BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ayodhya; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 200 BC; Disestablished: 100 BC; Preceded by: Maurya Empire; Succeeded by: Datta Dynasty

name: Kindah
description: Kindah was a prominent tribal Arab kingdom that originated in South Arabia before extending its influence across the central deserts and trade routes of the Arabian Peninsula. Operating from its prosperous commercial hub at Qaryat al-Faw, the kingdom served as a crucial intermediary between the sedentary civilisations of South Arabia and the nomadic tribes of the interior. Supported at times by the Himyarite monarchs to stabilise northern bedouin confederations, Kindah developed early administrative structures and written Arabic traditions before internal tribal fragmentation brought about its political decline in the mid-sixth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Qaryat al-Faw; Common languages: Old Arabic and Sabaic; Religion: South Arabian polytheism and Christianity; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hujrid dynasty; Historical era: Antiquity to Early Middle Ages; Established: 200 BC; Disestablished: 541

name: Mahameghavahana Dynasty
description: The Mahameghavahana Dynasty was an ancient ruling lineage that restored regional prominence to Kalinga along the eastern seaboard of India following the collapse of Mauryan hegemony. The dynasty reached its zenith during the first century BC under King Kharavela, whose celebrated Hathigumpha rock inscription records extensive military campaigns spanning the Deccan, Magadha and western India. Known for patronising Jainism while supporting diverse religious traditions, the rulers governed from the fortified city of Sisupalgarh until facing later pressures from the Satavahanas and eventual incorporation into the Gupta sphere. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Sisupalgarh; Common languages: Ardhamagadhi Prakrit and Sanskrit; Religion: Jainism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Kalingadhipati; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 200 BC; Disestablished: 376; Preceded by: Maurya Empire; Succeeded by: Gupta Empire

name: Principality of Ruhuna
description: The Principality of Ruhuna was an autonomous Sinhalese realm established across southern and eastern Sri Lanka around 200 BC by Prince Mahanaga following a succession rift in Anuradhapura. Governed from its capital at Tissamaharama, the principality nurtured a prosperous agricultural economy supported by extensive irrigation reservoirs and maritime trade along the southern coast. Serving as a resilient redoubt of Sinhalese culture and military power, Ruhuna frequently mobilised forces to liberate northern territories during periods of external invasion, notably providing the military base for King Dutugemunu's unification campaign in the second century BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Tissamaharama; Common languages: Early Sinhala; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Principality; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 200 BC; Disestablished: 137 BC; Succeeded by: Anuradhapura Kingdom

name: Saladoid
description: The Saladoid culture encompasses an expansive pre-Columbian ceramic tradition and maritime society that originated in the lower Orinoco River valley before colonising the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico. Organised in horticultural village communities without centralised urban seats, the Saladoid peoples navigated Caribbean waters in large dugout canoes, introducing settled root-crop farming and distinctive white-on-red painted ceramics to the islands. Their enduring tribal networks and communal village traditions shaped subsequent Taíno cultural developments across the West Indies over more than a millennium. \n\n Status: Tribal culture; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Arawakan languages; Religion: Indigenous animism and ancestor worship; Government: Tribal village confederacy; Historical era: Pre-Columbian Caribbean; Established: 200 BC; Disestablished: 1494

name: Samatata Kingdom
description: The Samatata Kingdom was an ancient geopolitical entity in the trans-Meghna region of the Bengal delta, encompassing much of present-day eastern and southern Bangladesh. Flourishing as an independent realm following the decline of Mauryan authority, the kingdom maintained thriving riverine and maritime commercial routes linking the Ganges-Brahmaputra estuary to Southeast Asian ports. Governed from regional administrative centres near modern Comilla, Samatata was a renowned stronghold of early Buddhist scholarship and monastic foundations prior to its recognition as a tributary border state in the Allahabad pillar inscription of Samudragupta. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Comilla; Common languages: Magadhan Prakrit and Sanskrit; Religion: Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 200 BC; Disestablished: 351; Succeeded by: Gupta Empire

name: Acarnanian League
label: antique greek leagues
description: The Acarnanian League was a federal confederacy of Greek poleis located in north-western Greece between the Achelous River and the Ionian Sea, operating under the patronage of the Roman Republic following the Second Macedonian War. Governed from its federal capital at Thyrreion, the league convened representative assemblies to oversee local justice, regional defence and religious festivals, while coordinating foreign relations strictly within the Roman sphere.
