This autonomous koinon endured for over a century and a half until Augustus dissolved the league after the Battle of Actium, incorporating its population into the newly founded colony of Nicopolis. \n\n Status: Roman client league; Capital: Thyrreion; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Federal republic; Historical era: Hellenistic to Roman period; Established: 197 BC; Disestablished: 32 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Empire

name: League of the Islanders
label: antique greek leagues
description: The League of the Islanders, known historically as the Second Nesiotic League, was a federal union of Aegean island city-states reconstituted under Rhodian hegemony in the wake of the Second Macedonian War. Centred around the sacred sanctuary island of Delos, the confederation aimed to secure maritime navigation, suppress regional piracy and promote commerce across the Cyclades under Rhodian naval oversight. The federal framework functioned effectively until Rome sought to undermine Rhodian commercial prominence following the Third Macedonian War, transforming Delos into a tax-free port and triggering the dissolution of the league around 167 BC. \n\n Status: Rhodian vassal league; Capital: Delos; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Federal confederacy; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 197 BC; Disestablished: 167 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Thessalian League
label: antique greek leagues
description: The Thessalian League was a federal state established across the fertile Thessalian plains in 196 BC after the Roman consul Titus Quinctius Flamininus proclaimed the freedom of Greece following Philip V of Macedon's defeat. Administered from its centre at Larissa under an elected general known as the strategos, the league issued federal silver coinage and managed regional agrarian affairs under Roman supervision. The confederacy maintained this client relationship throughout the Macedonian conflicts until Rome's annexation of Greece following the Achaean War reduced Thessaly to provincial administration in 147 BC. \n\n Status: Roman client league; Capital: Larissa; Common languages: Thessalian Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Federal republic; Ruler title: Strategos; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 196 BC; Disestablished: 147 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Joseon
description: Joseon, distinguished in historiography as Wiman Joseon, was an ancient Korean kingdom founded in 194 BC when the refugee Yan military officer Wiman usurped the Gojoseon throne from King Jun. Governed from the fortified city of Wanggeom-seong, on the site of modern Pyongyang, the realm commanded key trade routes linking the northern Chinese commanderies to the indigenous peoples of the southern Korean Peninsula. By leveraging advanced iron-working technology and expanding territorial control, the kingdom flourished until King Ugeo's refusal to permit direct Han trade prompted Emperor Wu to dispatch massive expeditionary armies that destroyed the state in 108 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Wanggeom-seong; Common languages: Old Korean and Old Chinese; Religion: Korean shamanism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Wiman dynasty; Historical era: Ancient Korea; Established: 194 BC; Disestablished: 108 BC; Preceded by: Gojoseon; Succeeded by: Four Commanderies of Han

name: Atropatene
description: Atropatene was an ancient Iranian kingdom centred in the rugged highlands of north-western Iran that functioned as a prominent vassal state under the Parthian Empire from the early second century BC. Ruled from the royal capital of Ganzak by the descendants of Atropates, the kingdom guarded strategic passes between the Iranian plateau and the southern Caucasus while preserving ancient Zoroastrian rites and sacred fires. Although formally subordinate to the Arsacid King of Kings, the monarchs exercised extensive internal autonomy until the campaigns of Tigranes the Great brought Atropatene into temporary Armenian subjugation around 88 BC. \n\n Status: Parthian vassal kingdom; Capital: Ganzak; Common languages: Old Azeri and Parthian; Religion: Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Atropatid dynasty; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 190 BC; Disestablished: 88 BC; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Armenia

name: Kingdom of Armenia
description: The Kingdom of Armenia during its sovereign Hellenistic era flourished as an independent monarchy founded by Artaxias I following the defeat of Antiochus III at Magnesia in 190 BC. Administered successively from Artashat and Tigranocerta, the kingdom reached imperial pre-eminence under Tigranes the Great, who unified historical Armenian lands and annexed swathes of Syria, Phoenicia and Mesopotamia. The state combined native Armenian culture and Zoroastrian traditions with Hellenistic urbanism and administrative institutions, maintaining sovereign authority across the highlands until Lucullus and Pompey enforced Roman terms in 66 BC, turning Armenia into a client realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Artashat and Tigranocerta; Common languages: Armenian, Greek and Aramaic; Religion: Zoroastrianism and Armenian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Artaxiad dynasty; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 190 BC; Disestablished: 66 BC; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Armenia (Roman client)

name: Corduene
description: Corduene, also known historically as Gordyene, was an ancient mountainous kingdom south of Lake Van along the upper reaches of the Tigris in what is now south-eastern Turkey. Emerging as an independent entity in the wake of weakening Seleucid authority following the Battle of Magnesia, the kingdom was inhabited by Carduchian tribes renowned for alpine archery and fortified hill settlements. Operating from its capital at Pinaka, Corduene navigated delicate diplomacy between Armenia and Parthia, maintaining sovereign self-rule until King Tigranes the Great forcibly annexed the territory into Greater Armenia around 90 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Pinaka; Common languages: Carduchian, Aramaic and Armenian; Religion: Polytheism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 189 BC; Disestablished: 90 BC; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Armenia

name: Kingdom of Sophene
description: The Kingdom of Sophene was an independent Hellenistic-era realm located in the fertile valleys between the upper Euphrates and Tigris rivers in south-eastern Anatolia. Proclaimed an autonomous kingdom by its governor Zariadres following the Roman defeat of the Seleucids at Magnesia in 189 BC, the state was ruled by a branch of the Orontid dynasty from its capital at Carcathiocerta. Sophene prospered from its position astride lucrative east-west caravan routes and exhibited a distinctive blend of Armenian, Greek and Persian cultural elements, retaining independence until Tigranes the Great conquered and absorbed the principality around 95 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Carcathiocerta; Common languages: Imperial Aramaic, Armenian and Greek; Religion: Zoroastrianism and Armenian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Orontid dynasty; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 189 BC; Disestablished: 95 BC; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Armenia

name: Shunga Empire
description: The Shunga Empire was a major Indian imperial state established around 185 BC when the commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Shunga assassinated the last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha in Magadha. Governed from Pataliputra alongside a second imperial court at Vidisha in eastern Malwa, the empire controlled vast swathes of the northern and central subcontinent, repelling Indo-Greek incursions along the north-western frontier. The Shungas sponsored Brahmanical traditions while simultaneously presiding over a brilliant flourishing of Buddhist sculpture and stone architecture, exemplified by monumental expansions at Sanchi and Bharhut, before being overthrown by the Kanva dynasty in 75 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Pataliputra and Vidisha; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Shunga dynasty; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 185 BC; Disestablished: 75 BC; Preceded by: Maurya Empire; Succeeded by: Kanva Dynasty

name: Beikthano
label: pyu city-states
description: Beikthano was one of the earliest and most prominent Pyu city-states, flourishing within the irrigated plains of the central Ayeyawady River basin in Upper Myanmar. Named in honour of the Hindu deity Vishnu, the city enclosed approximately three hundred hectares within massive baked-brick ramparts, featuring sophisticated gateway systems, elite residential compounds and early Buddhist stupas. The urban settlement served as a major centre of ceramic craft, ironworking and trans-regional riverine trade, pioneering architectural and funerary customs that influenced Pyu civilisation for centuries before its political pre-eminence was superseded by neighbouring centres like Sri Ksetra. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Beikthano; Common languages: Pyu; Religion: Buddhism, Hinduism and animism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical Southeast Asia; Established: 180 BC; Disestablished: 1051; Succeeded by: Pagan Kingdom

name: First Macedonian Meris
label: diadochi
description: The First Macedonian Meris was one of four client republics established by Rome across Macedonia following the defeat of King Perseus at Pydna in 168 BC. Governing the easternmost quadrant of the former Antigonid kingdom between the Strymon and Nestos rivers, the republic had its capital and mint at Amphipolis. Rome prohibited intermarriage and landholding between the different merides to suppress royalist resurgence, though each district retained an elected council. This fragmented republican experiment endured until the uprising of Andriscus prompted Rome to annex the region as a formal province in 147 BC. \n\n Status: Roman client republic; Capital: Amphipolis; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Aristocratic republic; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 169 BC; Disestablished: 147 BC; Preceded by: Antigonid Macedonia; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Fourth Macedonian Meris
label: diadochi
description: The Fourth Macedonian Meris was a client republic created by the Roman Senate in 167 BC from the upper western districts of fractured Antigonid Macedonia. Centred on the inland city of Pelagonia, the district incorporated mountainous borderlands adjacent to Illyria and Epirus, serving as a frontier buffer for Roman interests. While granted local self-governing assemblies and municipal revenue rights, citizens were barred from commercial ties with neighbouring merides. The republic's separate existence ended alongside the other Macedonian districts when Roman legions reorganised the territory into a unified province in 147 BC. \n\n Status: Roman client republic; Capital: Pelagonia; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Aristocratic republic; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 169 BC; Disestablished: 147 BC; Preceded by: Antigonid Macedonia; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Second Macedonian Meris
label: diadochi
description: The Second Macedonian Meris was a client republic established by Rome following the dismantlement of the Antigonid monarchy in the Third Macedonian War. Encompassing the Chalcidice peninsula and lands between the Strymon and Axios rivers, the district was governed from the commercial port of Thessaloniki. The republic held immense economic value due to its fertile agricultural hinterland, silver mines and maritime Aegean trade, though Roman decrees restricted inter-regional commerce. After maintaining this partitioned republican structure for two decades, Roman authorities dissolved the meris and absorbed its territory into the Roman province of Macedonia in 147 BC. \n\n Status: Roman client republic; Capital: Thessaloniki; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Aristocratic republic; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 169 BC; Disestablished: 147 BC; Preceded by: Antigonid Macedonia; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Third Macedonian Meris
label: diadochi
description: The Third Macedonian Meris was a client republic carved out of the historic heartland of Lower Macedonia by the Roman Senate following the Battle of Pydna. Headquartered at the traditional royal seat of Pella, the district stretched between the Axios and Peneus rivers, encompassing ancient palaces, wealthy agrarian plains and veteran settlements. Like the other three merides, it was governed by an elected representative council while forbidden from political alliances with adjacent districts. This artificial division proved unsustainable, culminating in regional rebellion under Andriscus and Rome's subsequent conversion of Macedonia into a formal province in 147 BC. \n\n Status: Roman client republic; Capital: Pella (Macedon); Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Aristocratic republic; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 169 BC; Disestablished: 147 BC; Preceded by: Antigonid Macedonia; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Lycian League
description: The Lycian League was an ancient democratic federal union of city-states along the Mediterranean coast of south-western Anatolia, operating as a protectorate of Rome following its release from Rhodian dominance in 168 BC. Governed from the maritime capital of Patara, the league functioned through a representative assembly with proportional voting rights based on city size. Member poleis shared mutual judicial bodies, common currency and coordinated defence while relying on Roman diplomatic guarantees, maintaining this autonomy until Emperor Claudius incorporated Lycia as an imperial Roman province in 44 AD. \n\n Status: Roman protectorate; Capital: Patara; Common languages: Ancient Greek and Lycian; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Federal republic; Legislature: Lykion koinon; Historical era: Hellenistic to Roman period; Established: 168 BC; Disestablished: 44; Succeeded by: Roman Empire

name: Adiabene
description: Adiabene was an ancient kingdom in northern Mesopotamia that gained sovereign independence around 164 BC amidst the rapid disintegration of Seleucid authority across the Near East. Centred between the Upper and Lower Zab rivers around the Assyrian stronghold of Arbela, the realm governed a strategic trade corridor linking upper Mesopotamia to the Iranian plateau. The kingdom established an autonomous administration and issued local coinage while balancing pressures from Armenia and neighbouring states, retaining sovereign status until King Mithridates I conquered the territory and incorporated Adiabene as a vassal of the Parthian Empire around 141 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Erbil; Common languages: Aramaic and Syriac; Religion: Mesopotamian polytheism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 164 BC; Disestablished: 141 BC; Preceded by: Seleucid Empire; Succeeded by: Parthian Empire

name: Rhodes
description: Rhodes functioned as a maritime republic and naval protectorate of Rome following the conclusion of a formal alliance in 164 BC. Headquartered at the harbour city of Rhodes, the island state commanded extensive merchant networks and preserved famous schools of philosophy, rhetoric and maritime law that attracted elite Roman students. Although stripped of its mainland holdings and eclipsed commercially by Delos, the republic retained municipal self-government and provided naval squadrons to Roman fleets until Emperor Vespasian annexed the island directly into the Roman Empire in 75 AD. \n\n Status: Roman protectorate; Capital: Rhodes; Common languages: Doric Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Aristocratic republic; Historical era: Hellenistic to Roman period; Established: 164 BC; Disestablished: 75; Succeeded by: Roman Empire

name: Kingdom of Timarchus
label: seleucid secessionist states
description: The Kingdom of Timarchus was a transient Hellenistic state established in Media in 163 BC when the Greek nobleman Timarchus, satrap of Media, declared independence following Antiochus IV Epiphanes' death. Ruling from the Iranian highland capital of Hamadan, Timarchus assumed the royal diadem, secured diplomatic recognition from the Roman Senate, and extended his dominion over Babylonia. His bid for imperial supremacy was cut short when King Demetrius I Soter marched east with a veteran army, defeating and executing Timarchus in 160 BC to reabsorb the eastern provinces into the Seleucid realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign rebel kingdom; Capital: Hamadan; Common languages: Ancient Greek and Median; Religion: Greek polytheism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 163 BC; Disestablished: 160 BC; Succeeded by: Seleucid Empire

name: Kingdom of Commagene
description: The Kingdom of Commagene was an autonomous Greco-Iranian buffer state that emerged along the upper Euphrates in 163 BC when the local satrap Ptolemaeus seceded from the fracturing Seleucid Empire. Governed from the fortified city of Samosata, the kingdom was ruled by a Hellenised branch of the Iranian Orontid dynasty who claimed proud descent from both Darius I of Persia and Alexander the Great. Commagene prospered by controlling vital river crossings and trade passes between Anatolia, Syria and Mesopotamia, developing a syncretic religious culture combining Persian and Greek divinities that culminated in monumental mountain sanctuaries like Nemrud Dagi. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Samosata; Common languages: Ancient Greek, Aramaic and Old Persian; Religion: Greco-Persian religious syncretism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Orontid dynasty; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 162 BC; Disestablished: 80 BC; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Armenia

name: Hasmonean Kingdom
description: The Hasmonean Kingdom was an independent Jewish state that arose from the successful Maccabean Revolt against the religious persecutions of the Seleucid Empire. Beginning with the campaigns of Judas Maccabeus and formalised under his brothers Jonathan and Simon, the Hasmoneans expelled foreign garrisons from Jerusalem, rededicated the Second Temple, and combined the office of High Priest with royal kingship. Through energetic military campaigns under John Hyrcanus and Alexander Jannaeus, the kingdom expanded across Samaria, Galilee, Idumaea and Perea, maintaining sovereignty until internal civil strife invited Roman intervention under Pompey in 63 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Jerusalem; Common languages: Hebrew, Aramaic and Koine Greek; Religion: Second Temple Judaism; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hasmonean dynasty; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 160 BC; Disestablished: 63 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Kingdom of Dayuan
label: greco-bactrian polities
description: The Kingdom of Dayuan was an urbanised Hellenistic realm in the fertile Fergana Valley of Central Asia, descending from Greek settlers established by Alexander the Great at Alexandria Eschate and earlier Persian deportees. Operating independently after nomadic migrations severed its links to the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom around 160 BC, Dayuan was noted for walled cities, prolific vineyards and prized heavenly horses. The kingdom's refusal to supply these horses to Han emissaries triggered a massive invasion under General Li Guangli, concluding in Dayuan's tributary submission to Han China in 101 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Ancient Greek and Eastern Iranian dialects; Religion: Greek polytheism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 160 BC; Disestablished: 101 BC; Succeeded by: Han dynasty

name: Bhojas of Goa
description: The Bhojas of Goa constituted an enduring ancient dynasty that governed Goa, coastal Konkan and adjacent sectors of Karnataka from the second century BC to the sixth century AD. Administering their coastal realm from Chandrapura, modern Chandor, the Bhoja rulers presided over vibrant maritime trade routes connecting Western Indian seaports to Indian Ocean commerce. As patrons of both Vedic Brahmanism and Buddhism, the dynasty issued royal copper-plate grants and governed as autonomous sovereigns or local feudatories under regional powers such as the Konkan Mauryas, until being displaced by the ascendant Chalukyas of Vatapi. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Goa Velha; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bhoja dynasty; Historical era: Classical to Early Medieval India; Established: 150 BC; Disestablished: 579; Succeeded by: Chalukyas of Badami

name: Chera Dynasty
description: The Chera Dynasty in its early historic Sangam period was one of the three crowned monarchies of Tamilakam, ruling over present-day Kerala and western Tamil Nadu. Governed from inland administrative centres such as Vanchi alongside bustling coastal port emporia at Muziris and Tyndis, the Cheras dominated the lucrative maritime spice trade, exporting black pepper, beryl and pearls to Graeco-Roman merchants. Their kingdom controlled strategic mountain transit corridors through the Palakkad Gap and Noyyal Valley, fostering early Tamil literary and artistic traditions before the onset of the obscure Kalabhra interregnum around the fourth century AD. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Old Tamil; Religion: Hinduism, Jainism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Sangam period; Established: 150 BC; Disestablished: 301; Succeeded by: Kalabhras

name: Indo-Scythian Kingdom
description: The Indo-Scythian Kingdom was an expansive realm established across Afghanistan, Pakistan and north-western India by migrating Saka tribes from Central Asia. Beginning in the second century BC under leaders like King Maues, the Sakas supplanted Indo-Greek rulers in Gandhara and the Indus Valley, synthesising Hellenistic administrative practices with nomadic traditions. Over subsequent centuries, the dynasty governed through semi-autonomous Northern and Western Satrapies, enduring conflicts with the Kushans and Satavahanas until the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II extinguished the final Saka satrap around 395 AD. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Taxila; Common languages: Saka, Prakrit, Sanskrit and Greek; Religion: Hinduism, Buddhism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King of Kings; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 150 BC; Disestablished: 396; Succeeded by: Gupta Empire

name: Satavahana Empire
description: The Satavahana Empire, identified as the Andhras in Puranic texts, was a paramount power that stabilised the Deccan plateau following the Maurya Empire's disintegration. Governing from capitals including Pratishthana and Amaravati, the dynasty spanned modern Maharashtra, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, resisting invasions from the Western Satraps and promoting maritime trade. The emperors patronised Prakrit literature, Vedic sacrificial rites and magnificent Buddhist rock-cut monasteries at Karle and Amaravati, ruling until internal fragmentation dissolved the realm into regional successor dynasties during the third century. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Paithan; Common languages: Maharashtri Prakrit and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Satavahana dynasty; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 150 BC; Disestablished: 228; Succeeded by: Western Kshatrapas and Andhra Ikshvaku

name: Kingdom of Elymais
description: The Kingdom of Elymais was an autonomous ancient state that re-established native Elamite sovereignty at the head of the Persian Gulf around 147 BC during the retreat of Seleucid power. Ruled by King Kamnaskires I Soter from the historic citadel of Susa and the Zagros foothills of Khuzestan, the state drew upon ancient Elamite heritage alongside Hellenistic administrative conventions and coinage. Kamnaskires controlled strategic trade corridors linking Mesopotamia to the Iranian interior, enjoying sovereign independence until the Parthian king Mithridates I invaded Susiana around 140 BC, reducing Elymais to a client realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Aramaic, Elamite and Greek; Religion: Elamite polytheism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kamnaskirid dynasty; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 147 BC; Disestablished: 140 BC; Succeeded by: Parthian Empire

name: Balearic Islands
description: The Balearic Islands experienced practical maritime independence across the western Mediterranean following the destruction of Carthage by Roman forces in 146 BC. Inhabited by Talaiotic communities renowned as elite mercenary slingers, the islands of Mallorca and Menorca operated autonomous tribal settlements and harbour redoubts outside formal imperial control. Their strategic position along sea routes between Hispania and Italy also made them a haven for Mediterranean piracy, prompting the Roman consul Quintus Caecilius Metellus to launch a naval expedition in 123 BC, establishing Roman provincial hegemony by 121 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal confederacy; Capital: Palma; Common languages: Paleohispanic dialects; Religion: Talaiotic polytheism; Government: Tribal confederacy; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 147 BC; Disestablished: 121 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Kingdom of Antioch
label: seleucid secessionist states
description: The Kingdom of Antioch was a separatist Hellenistic realm centred on the Syrian metropolis of Antioch, founded in 145 BC by the commander Diodotus Tryphon during the Seleucid dynastic wars. Initially revolting against Demetrius II Nicator as guardian for the infant Antiochus VI, Tryphon later deposed the prince and assumed the royal title of Autocrator, governing Syria and coastal Phoenicia. For several years he maintained sovereign authority across western Seleucid territories until Antiochus VII Sidetes invaded from abroad, trapping Tryphon in the fortress of Coracesium and driving him to suicide in 138 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign breakaway kingdom; Capital: Antioch; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Autocrator; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 145 BC; Disestablished: 138 BC; Succeeded by: Seleucid Empire

name: Characene
description: Characene, also recorded as Mesene, was an independent kingdom established at the head of the Persian Gulf in 141 BC by the Iranian noble Hyspaosines as Seleucid authority disintegrated in Lower Mesopotamia. Operating from the fortified riverine emporium of Charax Spasinu on the Tigris, the kingdom dominated lucrative maritime trade routes carrying Indian textiles and spices northward towards Babylon and the Mediterranean. Hyspaosines expanded his sway over Babylonia and Susa during a period of imperial weakness, issuing royal silver tetradrachms before being compelled to accept the suzerainty of Parthian king Mithridates II in 124 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Charax Spasinu; Common languages: Aramaic and Greek; Religion: Mesopotamian polytheism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hyspaosinid dynasty; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 141 BC; Disestablished: 124 BC; Succeeded by: Characene (Parthian vassal)

name: Yuezhi
description: The Yuezhi was an ancient nomadic confederation that established sovereign dominance over Central Asia and Bactria during the late second century BC following displacement by the Xiongnu from the Gansu grasslands. Migrating through the Ili Valley and across Sogdiana, the Greater Yuezhi overran the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom and divided the territory north of the Oxus into five autonomous tribal principalities. Maintaining a mobile pastoralist military ethos while utilising the agricultural resources of subject populations, the Yuezhi confederation laid the territorial groundwork for the eventual rise of the Kushan Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign nomadic confederation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Bactrian and Tocharian; Religion: Steppe shamanism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Nomadic confederation; Ruler title: Yabghu; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 140 BC; Disestablished: 101; Succeeded by: Kushan Empire

name: Kingdom of Osroene
description: The Kingdom of Osroene was an independent realm in Upper Mesopotamia established in 132 BC by an Arab chieftain named Aryu amidst the collapse of Seleucid authority along the northern Euphrates. Governed from the historic walled city of Edessa, now Şanlıurfa in south-eastern Turkey, the kingdom was ruled by the Arab Abgarid dynasty who oversaw a vital nexus of caravan commerce linking Syria, Armenia and Mesopotamia. Osroene balanced delicate diplomatic ties between the expanding Parthian Empire and regional powers, maintaining complete sovereignty until Tigranes the Great of Armenia expanded his hegemony over northern Mesopotamia around 88 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Şanlıurfa; Common languages: Classical Syriac and Aramaic; Religion: Mesopotamian and North Arabian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Abgarid dynasty; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 132 BC; Disestablished: 88 BC; Preceded by: Seleucid Empire; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Armenia

name: Yaudheya Republic
description: The Yaudheya Republic was a celebrated military ganasangha that flourished in the eastern plains of the Sapta Sindhu, in modern Haryana and adjoining parts of Rajasthan, following the decline of Mauryan rule. Renowned throughout ancient Indian literature as formidable warrior-clans dedicated to the martial deity Karttikeya, the Yaudheyas governed through an aristocratic assembly or sabha with its administrative seat at Rohitaka. They issued extensive copper and silver coinage celebrating their bravery and successfully repulsed invasions by Indo-Greeks and Indo-Scythians, maintaining their republican institutions for centuries until accepting the overarching suzerainty of the Gupta Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Rohitaka; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Aristocratic republic; Legislature: Sabhā; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 130 BC; Disestablished: 376; Succeeded by: Gupta Empire

name: Kangju
description: Kangju was a powerful semi-nomadic state in Central Asia that dominated the middle Syr Darya basin and neighbouring steppes of Transoxiana during the second century BC. Inhabited by an Eastern Iranian population affiliated with the Sogdians and Sakas, the realm commanded formidable cavalry forces and controlled northern trade corridors linking China to western Eurasia. Kangju maintained sovereign independence when visited by the Han envoy Zhang Qian around 128 BC, standing as a pre-eminent regional power alongside the Yuezhi until Han expeditions brought it into the Chinese tributary system in 101 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kangju; Common languages: Sogdian; Religion: Zoroastrianism and steppe animism; Government: Nomadic monarchy; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 128 BC; Disestablished: 101 BC; Succeeded by: Kangju (Chinese client)

name: Karasahr
label: tarim basin
description: Karasahr, known in native Tocharian inscriptions as Agni and in Chinese chronicles as Yanqi, was an ancient oasis kingdom along the northern Silk Road in the north-eastern Tarim Basin. Centred on the fertile oasis fed by the Kaidu River near Lake Bosten, the city-state was inhabited by Tocharian speakers who developed an urban culture based on irrigated agriculture, viticulture and trans-Eurasian trade. The kingdom enjoyed sovereign autonomy while balancing pressures from the nomadic Xiongnu confederation, until Han dynasty expeditions in 100 BC brought the oasis into the Chinese protectorate system. \n\n Status: Sovereign oasis kingdom; Capital: Yanqi; Common languages: Tocharian A and Gāndhārī; Religion: Buddhism and indigenous animism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 126 BC; Disestablished: 100 BC; Succeeded by: Karasahr (Chinese protectorate)

name: Loulan Kingdom
label: tarim basin
description: The Loulan Kingdom, known natively as Kroraina, was an ancient oasis state established around the lake of Lop Nur on the eastern threshold of the Tarim Basin. Inhabited by Tocharian-speaking communities, the kingdom commanded the vital nexus where Silk Road caravans entered China across the Lop Desert, supplying water, provisions and guides to merchants. While initially balancing relations with the nomadic Xiongnu, Loulan maintained independent diplomacy until intensifying Han interest in the Western Regions prompted General Zhao Ponu to invade in 108 BC, reducing the kingdom to a Han client. \n\n Status: Sovereign oasis kingdom; Capital: Loulan; Common languages: Tocharian and Gandhari; Religion: Buddhism and shamanism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 126 BC; Disestablished: 108 BC; Succeeded by: Loulan Kingdom (Chinese client)

name: Characene
description: Characene in this extended vassal phase operated as an autonomous client kingdom of the Parthian Empire, maintaining its commercial capital at Charax Spasinu on the lower Tigris. Under the suzerainty of the Arsacid King of Kings, Characene's rulers retained the privilege of minting their own coinage and commanded the principal maritime port connecting Roman Syrian trade with India. Despite periodic interventions from Rome, notably under Emperor Trajan in 116 AD, the kingdom preserved internal autonomy until the Sasanian founder Ardashir I conquered the realm in 224 AD. \n\n Status: Parthian vassal kingdom; Capital: Charax Spasinu; Common languages: Aramaic and Greek; Religion: Mesopotamian polytheism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hyspaosinid and Arsacid branches; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 124 BC; Disestablished: 28 April 224; Succeeded by: Sasanian Empire

name: Indo-Greek Kingdom
label: greco-bactrian polities
description: The Indo-Greek Kingdom comprised a succession of Hellenistic monarchies ruling across modern Pakistan, north-western India and eastern Afghanistan after nomadic migrations overran Bactria. Operating from major regional capitals such as Taxila and Sagala, monarchs like Menander I blended Greek and Indian governance, issuing bilingual coinage in Greek and Kharosthi while patronising Buddhism. This unique cultural synthesis, known as Greco-Buddhism, profoundly shaped regional sculpture and religious expression until successive incursions by Indo-Scythians and Indo-Parthians dismantled the final Greek enclaves in the early first century AD. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Taxila; Common languages: Koine Greek, Gandhari and Sanskrit; Religion: Greco-Buddhism, Greek polytheism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Basileus; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 120 BC; Disestablished: 11; Preceded by: Greco-Bactrian Kingdom; Succeeded by: Indo-Scythian Kingdom

name: Shule Kingdom
label: tarim basin
description: The Shule Kingdom was an ancient oasis city-state at the western extremity of the Tarim Basin, commanding the vital junction where the northern and southern Silk Roads converged before ascending the Pamir Mountains. Inhabited by Saka-speaking Eastern Iranian peoples who adhered to Buddhism, the kingdom was governed from its walled capital at Kashgar, sustained by the Kashgar River. Shule prospered as a primary commercial hub for trans-Eurasian trade, maintaining local monarchical governance and sovereign diplomacy until expanding Kushan imperial forces asserted regional hegemony in the early second century AD. \n\n Status: Sovereign oasis kingdom; Capital: Kashgar; Common languages: Saka and Tocharian; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 120 BC; Disestablished: 128; Succeeded by: Kushan Empire

name: Kingdom of Adherbal
description: The Kingdom of Adherbal was a Berber realm established across eastern Numidia in 116 BC following the death of King Micipsa and Rome's subsequent partition of the kingdom. Awarded the eastern territories alongside the royal capital of Cirta, Prince Adherbal struggled to preserve his sovereignty against his ambitious adoptive brother Jugurtha. Adherbal repeatedly petitioned the Roman Senate for diplomatic protection, but Jugurtha ignored Roman envoys, besieged Cirta in 112 BC, and executed Adherbal alongside resident Italian merchants, sparking the outbreak of the Jugurthine War. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Cirta (Adherbal); Common languages: Numidian, Punic and Latin; Religion: Traditional Berber religion and Punic polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Massylian dynasty; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 116 BC; Disestablished: 112 BC; Preceded by: Kingdom of Numidia; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Jugurtha

name: Kingdom of Jugurtha
description: The Kingdom of Jugurtha was a sovereign North African realm encompassing western Numidia, established in 116 BC after a Roman senatorial commission partitioned King Micipsa's realm. An astute military commander who had served with distinction at Numantia, Jugurtha commanded veteran Berber cavalry and sought to reunify all Numidia under his sole authority. In defiance of Roman diplomatic warnings, he invaded eastern Numidia in 112 BC, captured the capital of Cirta and eliminated his rival Adherbal, temporarily unifying the kingdom before facing a full-scale military conflict with Rome. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Constantine; Common languages: Numidian and Punic; Religion: Traditional Berber religion and Punic polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Massylian dynasty; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 116 BC; Disestablished: 112 BC; Preceded by: Kingdom of Numidia; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Numidia

name: Himyarite Kingdom
description: The Himyarite Kingdom was a pre-eminent South Arabian monarchy that emerged from the fragmentation of the Qatabanian realm around 110 BC, establishing its initial royal seat at Zafar in the Yemeni highlands. Through strategic military expansion and diplomacy, the Himyarites subdued neighbouring Saba, Qataban and Hadramawt, ultimately uniting the diverse kingdoms of ancient Yemen under the royal title of King of Saba and Dhu-Raydan. Controlling lucrative Red Sea maritime ports and Frankincense caravan corridors, the royal court embraced Judaism in the late fourth century before falling to an Aksumite invasion in 526 AD. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Zafar and Sana'a; Common languages: Himyarite and Sabaic; Religion: South Arabian polytheism and Judaism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Tubba; Historical era: Antiquity to Early Middle Ages; Established: 110 BC; Disestablished: 526; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Aksum

name: Eastern Ye
description: Eastern Ye, known in Korean sources as Dongye, was an ancient tribal chiefdom that occupied the coastal valleys and mountainous terrain of the north-eastern Korean Peninsula. Following the fall of Gojoseon and the establishment of Han China's Lelang Commandery in 108 BC, the Ye communities maintained internal autonomy organised under hereditary village headmen without a centralised urban capital. Renowned for their skilled archery, short bows, fine linen and maritime resources, the tribes celebrated the autumn agricultural festival of Mucheon while resisting northern encroachment from Goguryeo until their eventual absorption in the early third century. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal chiefdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Old Korean; Religion: Korean shamanism; Government: Tribal chiefdom; Historical era: Proto-Three Kingdoms period; Established: 108 BC; Disestablished: 205; Succeeded by: Goguryeo

name: Jushi Kingdom
label: tarim basin
description: The Jushi Kingdom was an ancient oasis state situated in the Turpan Basin of the eastern Tian Shan, operating as a client realm of Han China following General Zhao Ponu's expedition in 108 BC. Governed from the cliff-top fortress city of Jiaohe, perched between two deep river gorges, the Tocharian-speaking kingdom occupied a strategic crossroads along the northern Silk Road. Caught in protracted geopolitical rivalry between the Han dynasty and the nomadic Xiongnu, Jushi was repeatedly contested until Han forces established permanent protectorate administration in 60 BC. \n\n Status: Chinese client kingdom; Capital: Jiaohe; Common languages: Tocharian; Religion: Buddhism and shamanism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 108 BC; Disestablished: 60 BC; Succeeded by: Protectorate of the Western Regions

name: Loulan Kingdom
label: tarim basin
description: The Loulan Kingdom in this client phase operated under the strategic oversight of Han China following the successful desert expedition of General Zhao Ponu in 108 BC. Governed from its oasis capital at Loulan beside the fluctuating waters of Lop Nur, the kingdom was compelled to supply grain, postal couriers and military guides to Chinese caravans traversing the arid Tarim Basin. Due to continued diplomatic wavering and covert alliances between Loulan monarchs and the nomadic Xiongnu, Han emissaries assassinated King Angui in 77 BC, reorganising the state into the loyal client kingdom of Shanshan. \n\n Status: Chinese client kingdom; Capital: Loulan; Common languages: Tocharian and Gandhari; Religion: Buddhism and shamanism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 108 BC; Disestablished: 77 BC; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Shanshan

name: Kingdom of Numidia
description: The Kingdom of Numidia entered an era of clientage under the Roman Republic following the capture of King Jugurtha in 106 BC. Reorganised under Gauda and subsequently King Hiempsal II, the Berber monarchy was reduced in extent, with western lands ceded to Mauretania while remaining regions supported Roman commercial interests. The client state remained closely entangled in Roman factional wars, culminating when King Juba I aligned with Pompeian republicans against Julius Caesar, leading to Numidia's temporary provincial annexation after the Battle of Thapsus in 46 BC. \n\n Status: Roman client kingdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Numidian, Punic and Latin; Religion: Traditional Berber religion and Roman polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Massylian dynasty; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 106 BC; Disestablished: 25 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Empire and Kingdom of Mauretania

name: The Five Dravidians
description: The Five Dravidians denotes a sequence of five Tamil rulers, believed to have originated from the South Indian Pandya dynasty, who seized control of the Anuradhapura Kingdom in Sri Lanka in 103 BC. Displacing King Valagamba during a period of famine and foreign invasion, the chieftains ruled successively from the royal citadel of Anuradhapura over fourteen years. Each monarch was overthrown by his successor until the final ruler was defeated in 88 BC by the returning Valagamba, who restored the Sinhalese monarchy and established the great Abhayagiri Vihara. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Anuradhapura; Common languages: Old Tamil and Early Sinhala; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 103 BC; Disestablished: 88 BC; Preceded by: Anuradhapura Kingdom; Succeeded by: Anuradhapura Kingdom

name: Kangju
description: Kangju entered a tributary relationship with the Han Empire in 101 BC following General Li Guangli's Central Asian expedition against neighbouring Dayuan. Situated in the fertile valleys of the Syr Darya and across the Sogdian steppe, the semi-nomadic state maintained diplomatic ties and exchanged seasonal gifts with the imperial court while retaining internal sovereignty. Kangju leveraged this tributary status to safeguard lucrative trade networks, mediating between steppe confederations and oasis towns along the northern Silk Road until regional political fragmentation altered Central Asian alliances during the fifth century. \n\n Status: Chinese client kingdom; Capital: Kangju; Common languages: Sogdian; Religion: Zoroastrianism and steppe animism; Government: Nomadic monarchy; Historical era: Antiquity to Late Antiquity; Established: 101 BC; Disestablished: 501; Succeeded by: Hephthalite Empire

name: Audumbaras
description: The Audumbaras were an ancient Indian tribal republic established in the lower Himalayan foothills between the Beas and Yamuna rivers, in present-day Himachal Pradesh and eastern Punjab. Emerging as an independent political entity during the retreat of Indo-Greek hegemony around the first century BC, the community governed through a tribal council with an administrative seat near modern Hoshiarpur. The Audumbaras commanded important trade routes linking Himalayan valleys to the Gangetic plains, issuing distinct copper and silver coinage dedicated to the Vedic deity Shiva Mahadeva before their autonomy was subsumed by neighbouring powers. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal republic; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Aristocratic republic; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 49; Succeeded by: Western Satraps and Kushan Empire

name: Binnaka
label: pyu city-states
description: Binnaka was a prominent Pyu city-state established in the fertile agricultural zone of Upper Myanmar, situated in modern Pyawbwe Township near the Samon River. Inhabited by Tibeto-Burman Pyu communities from the late centuries BC, the fortified settlement featured elaborate brick masonry, extensive residential wards and sophisticated water-harvesting systems. Archaeological excavations have revealed rich assemblages of beads, metalwork and funerary urns that attest to vibrant commercial connections with neighbouring Pyu centres and Indian Ocean maritime networks. The city-state preserved its civic autonomy for centuries until being absorbed into the unifying Pagan Kingdom. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Binnaka; Common languages: Pyu; Religion: Buddhism, Hinduism and animism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical Southeast Asia; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 1051; Succeeded by: Pagan Kingdom

name: Buyeo
description: Buyeo was an ancient kingdom in northern Manchuria along the Songhua River basin, in what is now north-eastern China. Inhabited by the Yemaek people and governed by a hereditary monarch assisted by aristocratic chieftains named after domestic animals, the realm excelled in horse breeding, agriculture and iron metallurgy. Buyeo maintained diplomatic alliances with Han China to counterbalance the rise of Goguryeo, a kingdom founded by Buyeo exiles. Despite resilient resistance, the kingdom declined under nomad incursions before being formally absorbed by Goguryeo in 494 AD. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Buyeo; Common languages: Buyeo and Classical Chinese; Religion: Korean shamanism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hae dynasty; Historical era: Ancient Korea and Manchuria; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 495; Succeeded by: Goguryeo

name: Byeonhan Confederacy
description: The Byeonhan Confederacy was a loose alliance of tribal chiefdoms that occupied the lower Nakdong River valley in the southern Korean Peninsula. As one of the historic Samhan polities alongside Mahan and Jinhan, Byeonhan was renowned throughout East Asia for abundant iron ore deposits and advanced smelting technology, exporting iron ingots and weapons to Lelang and Yayoi Japan. The confederacy conducted commerce from coastal settlements near modern Gimhae, until political centralisation under King Suro transformed the alliance into the Gaya Confederacy in 42 AD. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal confederacy; Capital: Gimhae; Common languages: Han and Old Korean; Religion: Korean shamanism; Government: Tribal confederacy; Historical era: Proto-Three Kingdoms period; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 43; Succeeded by: Gaya Confederacy

name: Chi Tu Kingdom
description: The Chi Tu Kingdom, recorded in Sanskrit as Raktamrittika and in Chinese annals as the Red Earth Land, was an ancient Indianised realm situated on the Malay Peninsula around modern Songkhla and the Kelantan River. Positioned strategically along trans-peninsular portage routes, the kingdom flourished as a vital transhipment centre connecting Indian Ocean seafaring merchants with South China Sea trade networks. The royal court was characterised by sophisticated Buddhist and Brahmanical institutions, walled settlements and elaborate ceremonial embassies, sustaining its commercial prominence for centuries before being integrated into the maritime sphere of Srivijaya. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Songkhla; Common languages: Old Malay and Sanskrit; Religion: Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical to Medieval Southeast Asia; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 1201; Succeeded by: Srivijaya and Tambralinga

name: Datta Dynasty
description: The Datta Dynasty was an ancient Indian ruling lineage that governed the strategic city of Mathura along the Yamuna River during the first century BC. Succeeding the Deva dynasty in the wake of receding Indo-Greek authority, the rulers are documented through distinctive copper coinage bearing names such as Ramadatta and Seshadatta alongside images of Lakshmi. Mathura served as an important nexus for inland trade and religious patronage under their tenure, providing an administrative transition between post-Mauryan regional dynasties and the advent of the Indo-Scythian Northern Satraps. \n\n Status: Sovereign dynasty; Capital: Mathura; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Datta dynasty; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 1733; Succeeded by: Mitra Dynasty and Northern Satraps

name: Eastern Buyeo
description: Eastern Buyeo, known natively as Dongbuyeo, was an ancient Korean kingdom established along the Sea of Japan coast in south-eastern Manchuria and north-eastern Korea. According to historical traditions in the Samguk sagi, the kingdom originated when King Buru relocated the royal court eastward from ancestral Buyeo territories to evade nomadic pressure. Under rulers such as King Geumwa and King Daeso, Eastern Buyeo engaged in fierce political and military rivalries with the burgeoning state of Goguryeo, retaining its independence until the northern campaigns of King Gwanggaeto the Great forced its capitulation in 410 AD. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Tongcheon; Common languages: Buyeo; Religion: Korean shamanism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Buyeo royal line; Historical era: Ancient Korea; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 411; Preceded by: Buyeo; Succeeded by: Goguryeo

name: Halin
label: pyu city-states
description: Halin was a paramount Pyu city-state situated in the irrigated belt of the Mu River valley near modern Shwebo in Upper Myanmar. Flourishing from the late first millennium BC, the settlement enclosed a massive area within monumental brick ramparts protected by moats, curved gateways and watchtowers. Halin functioned as a centre of ironworking, bead manufacture, Buddhist learning and trade along routes connecting India to south-western China. It stood as the pre-eminent metropolis of the Pyu realm until warfare prompted a shift of regional influence southward to Sri Ksetra. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Halin; Common languages: Pyu; Religion: Buddhism, Hinduism and animism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical Southeast Asia; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 871; Succeeded by: Sri Ksetra

name: Jinhan Confederacy
description: The Jinhan Confederacy was an ancient league of twelve autonomous chiefdoms that occupied the eastern Nakdong River basin in south-eastern Korea during the Proto-Three Kingdoms period. Functioning as one of the three Samhan federations alongside Mahan and Byeonhan, Jinhan developed intensive rice agriculture, sericulture and metallurgy while maintaining defensive earthworks around municipal settlements. The leading member of the confederacy, the city-state of Saro centred at modern Gyeongju, gradually consolidated administrative dominance over its peers, directly evolving into the unified kingdom of Silla during the fourth century AD. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal confederacy; Capital: Gyeongju; Common languages: Han and Old Korean; Religion: Korean shamanism; Government: Tribal confederacy; Historical era: Proto-Three Kingdoms period; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 351; Succeeded by: Silla

name: Karasahr
label: tarim basin
description: Karasahr functioned as a strategic client oasis state within the Western Regions protectorate system of Han China from 100 BC until the late first century AD. Headquartered at the fortified town of Yanqi along the Kaidu River, the Tocharian-speaking kingdom supplied provisions, scouts and cavalry contingents to Han garrisons along the northern Silk Road. The oasis kings preserved domestic governance and Buddhist practices, but were compelled to maintain hostage princes at the Han court and support campaigns against the Xiongnu, until regional rebellions dissolved Chinese oversight in 74 AD. \n\n Status: Chinese protectorate; Capital: Yanqi; Common languages: Tocharian A and Gāndhārī; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 74; Preceded by: Karasahr (sovereign); Succeeded by: Karasahr (sovereign)

name: Kingdom of Munster
label: irish medieval kingdoms;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Munster was a major Gaelic kingdom in south-western Ireland that traced its origins to Iron Age tribal lineages of the Clanna Dedad. Governed from royal inauguration sites including the Rock of Cashel, the realm was dominated for centuries by the Eóganachta before the rise of the Dál gCais under Brian Boru altered Irish dynastic politics. Munster fostered Brehon law, monastic scholarship and Christian art while resisting Viking incursions, enduring until Anglo-Norman invasions fragmented the territory into Thomond and Desmond in the late twelfth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign Gaelic kingdom; Capital: Cashel; Common languages: Old Irish and Middle Irish; Religion: Celtic Christianity and Catholicism; Government: Tanistry monarchy; Ruler title: Rí; Historical era: Antiquity to High Middle Ages; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 1172; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Thomond and Kingdom of Desmond

name: Mahan Confederacy
description: The Mahan Confederacy was the largest of the three Samhan federations, encompassing over fifty autonomous tribal chiefdoms across south-western Korea in Chungcheong and Jeolla provinces. Headquartered nominally at the chiefdom of Mokji near present-day Iksan, the confederacy developed wet-rice agriculture, communal walled villages and seasonal rituals dedicated to ancestral spirits. Among the northern constituent polities of the league, the emergent kingdom of Baekje rapidly consolidated military power, progressively subduing adjacent chiefdoms until King Geunchogo fully absorbed the remaining Mahan territories into the centralised Baekje state in 376 AD. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal confederacy; Capital: Iksan; Common languages: Han and Old Korean; Religion: Korean shamanism; Government: Tribal confederacy; Historical era: Proto-Three Kingdoms period; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 376; Succeeded by: Baekje

name: Maingmaw
label: pyu city-states
description: Maingmaw was an ancient Pyu city-state located in the fertile Kyaukse plains of Upper Myanmar, positioned strategically near the confluence of the Irrawaddy and Samon rivers. Characterised by an unusual plan featuring an outer circular earthen rampart enclosing an inner rectangular brick fortress, the city was engineered to manage complex irrigation networks supporting intensive paddy farming. Maingmaw flourished as an early centre of Buddhist worship, bead production and metal smelting, maintaining vibrant regional trade links across central Burma throughout the Pyu millennium until being incorporated into the unified realm of the Pagan Kingdom. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Maingmaw; Common languages: Pyu; Religion: Buddhism, Hinduism and animism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical Southeast Asia; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 1051; Succeeded by: Pagan Kingdom

name: Mitra Dynasty
description: The Mitra Dynasty was an ancient Indian ruling lineage based in the historic city of Kosambi, governing the prosperous Vatsa region in the middle Gangetic valley from the first century BC. Emerging following the fragmentation of the Shunga Empire, the dynasty is documented through copper coinage bearing royal names ending in mitra alongside symbols of a bull and a tree-in-railing. The monarchs presided over a major commercial hub linking northern riverine trade to southern caravan routes, maintaining sovereignty until Samudragupta annexed Kosambi into the Gupta Empire in the fourth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign dynasty; Capital: Kosambi; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Mitra dynasty; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 351; Preceded by: Shunga Empire; Succeeded by: Gupta Empire

name: Oddiyana
description: Oddiyana was an ancient mountain kingdom established in the fertile, secluded valley of the Swat River in what is now northern Pakistan. Positioned along alpine passes connecting Gandhara to the Pamir plateau and the Tarim Basin, the kingdom flourished as a vital spiritual and commercial crossroads during the post-Mauryan era. Governed from its historic capital at Manglawar, Oddiyana became internationally celebrated throughout Buddhist traditions as a sacred heartland for the development of early tantric philosophy and scholastic learning, maintaining sovereign independence until being incorporated into the expanding Indo-Scythian realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Manglawar; Common languages: Gandhari and Sanskrit; Religion: Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 50 BC; Succeeded by: Indo-Scythian Kingdom

name: Proto-Nazca Culture
description: The Proto-Nazca Culture represents an early formative Andean archaeological society that flourished across the arid river valleys of the Rio Grande de Nazca and Ica along the southern coast of Peru. Developing out of the earlier Paracas ceramic and textile traditions, the culture was organised in agrarian settlements and ceremonial gathering centres without a centralised urban capital. The inhabitants constructed sophisticated underground aqueduct channels known as puquios to irrigate desert soils, engineered monumental polychrome pottery with mythological iconography, and laid the social foundations for the subsequent development of the classic Nazca geoglyphs. \n\n Status: Tribal culture; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Pre-Incan Andean languages; Religion: Indigenous Andean polytheism; Government: Theocratic tribal society; Historical era: Early Intermediate Period; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 2; Preceded by: Paracas culture; Succeeded by: Nazca culture

name: Sri Ksetra
label: pyu city-states
description: Sri Ksetra, meaning the Field of Glory in Sanskrit, was the largest and most influential Pyu city-state, situated along the lower Irrawaddy River near modern Pyay in central Myanmar. Enclosed by massive circular brick fortifications encompassing over fourteen hundred hectares, the city featured monumental stupas, grand palace enclosures and sophisticated hydraulic engineering works. Sri Ksetra served as a renowned beacon of Theravada Buddhist scholarship, Pali script literacy and vibrant Indian Ocean commerce, setting the cultural and religious standards of the Pyu millennium until its dominance was eventually absorbed by the burgeoning Pagan Kingdom. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Pyay; Common languages: Pyu, Sanskrit and Pali; Religion: Buddhism, Hinduism and animism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical Southeast Asia; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 1051; Succeeded by: Pagan Kingdom

name: Teotihuacan
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Teotihuacan was a monumental pre-Columbian urban civilisation in the north-eastern Valley of Mexico, growing to become the largest metropolis in the ancient Americas. Laid out along the ceremonial axis of the Avenue of the Dead, the city was anchored by the colossal Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon, accommodating an estimated multi-ethnic population of one hundred thousand in complex residential compounds. Teotihuacan projected extensive commercial, artistic and military influence across Mesoamerica, exporting green obsidian and influencing distant Maya dynastic politics before suffering destruction and abandonment around 541 AD. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Teotihuacan; Common languages: Mesoamerican languages (possibly Nahuan, Totonacan or Otomian); Religion: Teotihuacan polytheism; Government: Theocratic oligarchy; Historical era: Classic Mesoamerica; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 541

name: Tilantongo
description: Tilantongo was a prominent Mixtec city-state and sacred ceremonial centre in the rugged highlands of the Mixteca Alta in modern Oaxaca. Occupied continuously from the Late Preclassic period until the Spanish conquest in 1522, the city served as the paramount dynastic seat of the Mixtec people, celebrated in pictorial codices for royal marriage alliances and ritual warfare. Under the eleventh-century ruler Lord Eight Deer Jaguar Claw, Tilantongo unified the Mixteca kingdoms into an expansive regional realm, preserving its autonomous indigenous lordship until the arrival of the Spanish conquistadors. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Tilantongo; Common languages: Mixtec; Religion: Mixtec polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Yya; Historical era: Classic to Postclassic Mesoamerica; Established: 100 BC; Disestablished: 1522; Succeeded by: Spanish Empire

name: Italic League
description: The Italic League was a revolutionary confederation formed in 91 BC by autonomous Italian allies, primarily the Marsi and Samnites, in armed rebellion against the Roman Republic during the Social War. Establishing their federal capital at Corfinium, which they renamed Italica, the allies created an alternative senate, appointed two consuls and issued silver coinage depicting the Italian bull goring the Roman wolf. The league fielded disciplined armies that inflicted severe defeats on Roman legions, compelling Rome to concede Roman citizenship to Italian allies before crushing the final rebel strongholds in 88 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign confederation; Capital: Corfinium; Common languages: Oscan, Umbrian and Latin; Religion: Italic polytheism; Government: Federal republic; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 92 BC; Disestablished: 88 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Kingdom of Dacia
description: The Kingdom of Dacia was a powerful Iron Age monarchy unified around 82 BC by King Burebista, who consolidated the Dacian and Getae tribes across modern Romania and the Carpathian valleys. Anchored by the mountain citadel of Sarmizegetusa Regia, the kingdom developed sophisticated stone hill-fortresses, rich gold mining and religious sanctuaries dedicated to Zalmoxis. Under King Decebalus, Dacia fiercely resisted Roman expansion across the Danube, until Emperor Trajan waged two massive campaigns that annihilated the realm in 106 AD, converting Dacia into an imperial Roman province. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Sarmizegetusa; Common languages: Dacian; Religion: Zalmoxianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 82 BC; Disestablished: 1 September 106; Succeeded by: Roman Empire

name: Kingdom of Aksum
description: The Kingdom of Aksum was a major commercial and naval empire based in the highlands of modern Eritrea and northern Ethiopia, commanding maritime routes between the Roman Empire and India. Governed from its capital at Aksum through its Red Sea port of Adulis, the state exported ivory, gold and frankincense while issuing its own gold coinage. Under King Ezana in the fourth century, the empire embraced Christianity and erected towering monolithic stelae, projecting military power across the Red Sea into South Arabia before maritime isolation contributed to its collapse in the tenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Aksum; Common languages: Ge'ez, Sabaic and Greek; Religion: Semitic polytheism, later Oriental Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Negus; Historical era: Classical antiquity to Early Middle Ages; Established: 80 BC; Disestablished: 961; Succeeded by: Zagwe dynasty

name: Kingdom of Cyprus
label: diadochi
description: The Kingdom of Cyprus was an independent Hellenistic monarchy established in 80 BC when Ptolemaic domains were divided between the sons of Ptolemy IX. While Ptolemy XII took the Egyptian throne, his younger brother Ptolemy of Cyprus was installed as sovereign monarch over the entire island from his capital at Paphos. The kingdom governed the copper-rich island autonomously for over two decades, maintaining administrative peace and accumulating substantial royal treasure. This sovereign period ended in 58 BC when the Roman Republic dispatched Cato the Younger to annex the island, driving King Ptolemy to suicide. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Paphos; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ptolemaic dynasty; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 80 BC; Disestablished: 58 BC; Preceded by: Ptolemaic Kingdom; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Mitra Dynasty
description: The Mitra Dynasty of Mathura was an autonomous ruling house that governed the commercial and sacred centre of Mathura along the Yamuna River during the middle of the first century BC. Succeeding the Datta dynasty, the monarchs issued copper coins bearing names with the suffix mitra, depicting traditional religious motifs without explicit imperial titles. Their sovereign rule provided stability and patronage for Hindu, Buddhist and Jain communities in the northern plains, until the emerging Indo-Scythian Northern Satraps established hegemony over Mathura around 60 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign dynasty; Capital: Mathura; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism, Jainism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Mitra dynasty; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 80 BC; Disestablished: 60 BC; Preceded by: Datta Dynasty; Succeeded by: Northern Satraps

name: Kanva Dynasty
description: The Kanva Dynasty was an ancient Indian ruling house that established control over Magadha and eastern Malwa around 75 BC after the minister Vasudeva Kanva assassinated the last Shunga monarch Devabhuti. Governing from Pataliputra alongside a primary court at Vidisha, the four successive Kanva emperors maintained the administrative apparatus of the central plains while permitting the Shungas to rule minor subordinate fiefs. Devout patrons of Brahmanical religion, the dynasty presided over four decades of regional stability until an offensive by the Satavahana Empire extinguished the realm around 30 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Patna and Besnagara; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kanva dynasty; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 75 BC; Disestablished: 30 BC; Preceded by: Shunga Empire; Succeeded by: Satavahana Empire

name: Arjunayana Republic
description: The Arjunayana Republic was an ancient aristocratic ganasangha that established regional autonomy across north-eastern Rajasthan and southern Haryana following the Shunga Empire's decline around 73 BC. Tracing their legendary descent from the epic warrior Arjuna, the Arjunayanas governed through a representative assembly known as the sabha. The republic commanded trade corridors south of Delhi, minting characteristic copper coinage celebrating the martial valour of their community. They preserved their republican institutions through centuries of regional upheavals, finally acknowledging the tributary overlordship of the Gupta Empire during the fourth century AD. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Aristocratic republic; Legislature: Sabhā; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 73 BC; Disestablished: 351; Succeeded by: Gupta Empire

name: Seleucid Kingdom
description: The Seleucid Kingdom in this final phase existed as a fragile Roman client state in northern Syria, restored in 69 BC by the Roman general Lucullus under King Antiochus XIII Asiaticus following the retreat of Tigranes the Great. Confined to the royal metropolis of Antioch on the Orontes, the rump monarchy was paralysed by dynastic infighting against rival claimant Philip II Barypos and Arab border incursions. Recognising that the decaying dynasty could no longer secure the frontier against Parthia, the Roman general Pompey deposed Antiochus XIII in 63 BC, annexing Syria as a Roman province. \n\n Status: Roman protectorate; Capital: Antakya; Common languages: Ancient Greek and Aramaic; Religion: Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Seleucid; Historical era: Hellenistic period; Established: 69 BC; Disestablished: 63 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Colchis
description: Colchis was an ancient Black Sea kingdom centred across the fertile valleys of western Georgia, functioning as a Roman vassal following Pompey's Caucasian campaign in 66 BC. Celebrated in classical mythology as the land of the Golden Fleece, the kingdom was inhabited by indigenous Zan-speaking tribes and administered from strongholds along the Phasis River. Pompey installed the local noble Aristarchus as dynast under Roman suzerainty, issuing silver drachms and securing the eastern Pontic maritime frontier. The client state preserved local governance until Emperor Nero incorporated the territory directly into the Roman provincial administration. \n\n Status: Roman vassal kingdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Zan and Ancient Greek; Religion: Georgian polytheism and Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 66 BC; Disestablished: 65; Succeeded by: Roman Empire

name: Corduene
description: Corduene functioned as an autonomous client kingdom of Rome following Pompey's settlement of the Near East in 66 BC. Located in the rugged mountainous terrain south of Lake Van along the upper Tigris, the realm was governed from its fortified seat at Pinaka by native Carduchian dynasts. Corduene occupied a crucial strategic buffer between the Roman sphere, Armenia and the Parthian Empire, providing Roman commanders with mountain auxiliaries and frontier surveillance. The client state retained its domestic governance until intensifying Parthian rivalries altered regional administration in the first century AD. \n\n Status: Roman vassal kingdom; Capital: Pinaka; Common languages: Carduchian, Aramaic and Armenian; Religion: Polytheism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 66 BC; Disestablished: 38; Succeeded by: Roman Empire and Kingdom of Armenia

name: Kingdom of Armenia
description: The Kingdom of Armenia in this client phase operated under the strategic hegemony of Rome following King Tigranes the Great's submission to Pompey in 66 BC. Permitted to retain his ancestral crown while ceding conquests in Syria and Mesopotamia, Tigranes governed from Artaxata as a recognised ally of the Roman people. Armenia served as the paramount buffer monarchy between the Roman and Parthian empires, with both powers constantly vying to install favoured candidates upon the throne until the kingdom's formal partition in the late fourth century. \n\n Status: Roman client kingdom; Capital: Artaxata; Common languages: Armenian, Greek and Parthian; Religion: Zoroastrianism, later Armenian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Artaxiad and Arsacid dynasties; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 66 BC; Disestablished: 385; Succeeded by: Roman Empire and Sasanian Empire

name: Kingdom of Commagene
description: The Kingdom of Commagene was an autonomous Roman client state along the upper Euphrates, entering Rome's geopolitical orbit in 66 BC when King Antiochus I Theos concluded an alliance with Pompey. Governing from the fortified river capital of Samosata, the Orontid monarchs controlled crucial Euphrates crossing points and maintained a magnificent mountain sanctuary at Mount Nemrud. The wealthy buffer kingdom rendered military auxiliaries and financial subsidies to Roman campaigns against Parthia, maintaining local self-rule until Emperor Vespasian annexed the realm into the province of Syria in 73 AD. \n\n Status: Roman client kingdom; Capital: Samosata; Common languages: Ancient Greek, Aramaic and Old Persian; Religion: Greco-Persian religious syncretism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Orontid dynasty; Historical era: Hellenistic to Roman period; Established: 66 BC; Disestablished: 73; Succeeded by: Roman Empire

name: Caucasian Albania
description: Caucasian Albania operated as a client state of Rome following the victorious Caucasian expeditions of Pompey in 65 BC. Governing the fertile plains between the Kura River and the Caspian Sea from the royal seat at Kabalak, the indigenous Albanian monarchy retained its tribal hierarchy and local laws while guarding the Caspian Gates against northern nomadic incursions. Roman diplomatic missions and military detachments periodically reinforced imperial influence over the kingdom, until the rising Sasanian Empire asserted permanent dominion over the eastern Caucasus during the third century. \n\n Status: Roman client kingdom; Capital: Kabalak; Common languages: Caucasian Albanian and Parthian; Religion: Caucasian Albanian polytheism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 65 BC; Disestablished: 348; Succeeded by: Sasanian Empire

name: Kingdom of Iberia
description: The Kingdom of Iberia, known natively as Kartli, was an ancient Georgian realm in eastern Georgia that became a Roman client kingdom in 65 BC after Pompey defeated King Artag. Administered from the fortified capital of Mtskheta, the kingdom occupied a vital geopolitical position commanding the Darial Gorge across the Greater Caucasus. The Iberian monarchs maintained close military alliances with Rome, supplying cavalry to counter Parthian ambitions and receiving imperial subsidies from Roman emperors, before shifting into the Sasanian sphere during the late antique Persian wars. \n\n Status: Roman client kingdom; Capital: Mtskheta; Common languages: Old Georgian and Greek; Religion: Georgian paganism, later Georgian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Artaxiad, Arsacid and Pharnavazid branches; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 65 BC; Disestablished: 528; Succeeded by: Sasanian Empire and Byzantine Empire

name: Kingdom of Lesser Armenia
description: The Kingdom of Lesser Armenia, situated west of the upper Euphrates in eastern Anatolia, was reorganised as a client monarchy of the Roman Republic following Pompey's settlement of the Mithridatic Wars in 65 BC. Governing the mountainous highlands along the Roman eastern frontier, the kingdom was repeatedly granted by the Roman Senate to trusted client dynasts to secure strategic routes leading into Greater Armenia. The realm provided valuable military auxiliaries and preserved frontier stability against Parthian incursions, retaining its autonomous status until Emperor Vespasian integrated Lesser Armenia into the province of Cappadocia in 73 AD. \n\n Status: Roman vassal kingdom; Capital: Kozan; Common languages: Armenian and Ancient Greek; Religion: Armenian polytheism and Greek polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 65 BC; Disestablished: 73; Succeeded by: Roman Empire

name: Kingdom of Emesa
description: The Kingdom of Emesa was an influential Roman client realm established in central Syria in 64 BC when the Roman general Pompey confirmed the Arab chieftain Sampsigeramus I as ruler. Governed by the hereditary Sampsigeramid dynasty of priest-kings, the state was centred on the Orontes River valley around modern Homs, where the monarchs presided over the celebrated cult of the sun god Elagabal. The Emesene rulers rendered staunch military assistance to Roman armies during regional campaigns, retaining their domestic autonomy until Emperor Domitian incorporated the principality into the Roman province of Syria around 79 AD. \n\n Status: Roman client kingdom; Capital: Homs; Common languages: Aramaic and Ancient Greek; Religion: Emesene sun-worship and North Arabian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sampsigeramid dynasty; Historical era: Hellenistic to Roman period; Established: 64 BC; Disestablished: 79; Succeeded by: Roman Empire
